lessons.title: What each network layer does
lessons.summary: Distinguish the OSI, TCP/IP and five-layer models and identify each layer’s responsibility.
lessons.body:
Sending a web page from a server in Frankfurt to your phone involves electrical pulses, radio waves, error checks, addresses, routing decisions, retransmissions, encryption and HTTP. Dividing these responsibilities makes the system easier to build and reason about.

Networks tame this by **layering**. In the model, each layer groups related responsibilities, relies on services below, and offers a cleaner service to the layer above. Ethernet does not care whether it carries a web page or a video call. HTTP does not care whether the bits travel over fibre or Wi-Fi.

This lesson sets up the vocabulary used for the rest of the subject.

## The two models

There are two reference models you will meet constantly.

The **OSI reference model** has seven layers. Its *numbering* survived: engineers still say "layer 2 switch" or "layer 7 load balancer".

The **TCP/IP model** (described in RFC 1122) has four layers and describes the protocols the internet actually runs.

| # | OSI layer | TCP/IP layer | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | Application | Application | HTTP, DNS, SMTP |
| 6 | Presentation | Application | TLS, encodings |
| 5 | Session | Application | (rarely distinct) |
| 4 | Transport | Transport | TCP, UDP; QUIC over UDP |
| 3 | Network | Internet | IP, ICMP |
| 2 | Data link | Link | Ethernet, Wi-Fi |
| 1 | Physical | Link | Cables, radio |

Many textbooks (Kurose and Ross, Tanenbaum) teach a hybrid **five-layer** model: physical, link, network, transport, application. That is the model this subject follows.

A basic Ethernet bridge doing ordinary layer-2 forwarding within one VLAN looks up the destination MAC address. It does not need an IP destination or an application header for that lookup.

What each layer is responsible for:

- **Physical**: turn bits into signals on a medium and back again.
- **Link**: move a frame across *one* link or LAN to the next device, using link-specific framing and, on Ethernet or Wi-Fi, MAC addresses.
- **Network**: move a packet from source host to destination host across many links, using IP addresses and routing; not all IP addresses are globally routable or uniquely identify one host.
- **Transport**: deliver data between transport endpoints using ports and addresses. Services vary: TCP offers an ordered reliable byte stream and congestion control; UDP itself does not.
- **Application**: whatever the program needs: fetching pages, resolving names, sending mail.

> [!tip] Hop-by-hop versus end-to-end
> Layers 1 and 2 operate on a single hop. Layer 3 crosses the whole path, but every router along the way inspects it. Layers 4 and up are, in principle, only looked at by the two end hosts. Remembering this explains a lot about which devices touch which headers.

## Key takeaways
- The OSI numbering describes seven responsibilities; this course uses the five-layer teaching model.
- Link delivery is local to a hop or LAN; network routing crosses links.

questions.prompt: For ordinary layer-2 destination forwarding within one VLAN, which address does a basic Ethernet bridge look up?

options.text: The IP header's destination address
options.explanation: IP destination lookup is a routing function. This question isolates ordinary bridging; real switches may implement routing and filtering too.

options.text: The Ethernet header's destination MAC address
options.explanation: Correct. It looks up the destination MAC within the VLAN’s forwarding context. Unknown unicast or broadcast traffic can be flooded rather than sent to one known port.

options.text: The TCP header's destination port
options.explanation: TCP ports can be inspected for filtering or load distribution, but are not the address used in the basic bridge lookup asked about here.

options.text: The HTTP Host header
options.explanation: HTTP Host can guide an application proxy, not this basic MAC-table lookup.

questions.workedExample: For this ordinary bridging lookup, the switch uses the destination MAC and VLAN forwarding context. It need not inspect IP, TCP or HTTP to make that decision. Other functions on the same device may still inspect higher layers.

questions.prompt: An application library handles character encoding and maintains a login session above TCP. In the four-layer TCP/IP model, where do these responsibilities belong?

options.text: Application
options.explanation: Correct. TCP/IP groups these higher-level responsibilities into its application layer.

options.text: Transport
options.explanation: TCP provides a byte-stream service; it does not interpret character encodings or application login sessions.

options.text: Internet
options.explanation: IP addresses and routes packets rather than interpreting a login session.

options.text: Link
options.explanation: Local framing and medium access do not determine an application's text representation.

questions.workedExample: Ask what the operation understands. Character encoding and login state require application meaning. TCP delivers bytes without interpreting them, while IP and link services move the containing packets and frames. The TCP/IP application layer therefore includes work that the OSI model separates into presentation and session responsibilities.

lessons.title: Encapsulation and protocol selection
lessons.summary: Follow a payload through headers and learn how receivers select the next protocol.
lessons.body:
## Encapsulation

On the way down the stack, each layer takes what the layer above handed it, treats it as an opaque **payload**, and adds its own **header** in front (and sometimes appends a trailer). On the way up at the receiver, each layer strips its header, acts on it, and passes the payload up.

Each layer's unit has a name, the **PDU** (protocol data unit):

| Layer | PDU name |
|---|---|
| Application | Message |
| Transport | Segment (TCP) / datagram (UDP) |
| Network | Packet (or datagram) |
| Link | Frame |
| Physical | Bits / symbols |

```diagram
App            [   HTTP data   ]
Transport  [TCP][   HTTP data   ]
Network [IP][TCP][   HTTP data   ]
Link [Eth][IP][TCP][ HTTP data ][FCS]
```

### How the receiver knows what is inside

Several headers and endpoint identifiers allow **demultiplexing**, selecting the next protocol or recipient. Not every protocol header contains an explicit next-protocol field:

- Ethernet's **EtherType** field: `0x0800` means IPv4, `0x86DD` IPv6, `0x0806` ARP.
- IPv4's **Protocol** field (IPv6 calls it Next Header): `6` is TCP, `17` UDP, `1` ICMPv4 and `58` ICMPv6. IPv6 Next Header can also identify an extension header.
- TCP and UDP **port numbers**, together with addresses and other socket context, select transport endpoints. Port 443 conventionally serves HTTPS and 53 serves DNS; port numbers alone do not prove the application protocol or uniquely identify one process.

Without these fields a receiver would see an undifferentiated stream of bytes.

For ordinary forwarding without NAT or a tunnel, each router replaces the incoming link-layer frame for the next link while preserving the source and destination IP addresses. It decrements IPv4 TTL (or IPv6 Hop Limit); an IPv4 router also updates the IPv4 header checksum. These changes do not normally change the transport ports. A basic bridge forwarding within one VLAN instead looks up the destination MAC address.

## Key takeaways
- EtherType and IP protocol fields identify payload protocols.
- Each routed Ethernet hop needs its own local frame; end hosts interpret transport endpoints.

## Further reading
- [RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122)
- [OSI model — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSI_model)
- [Internet protocol suite — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_protocol_suite)
- [Encapsulation (networking) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encapsulation_(networking))
- [RFC 3439: Some Internet Architectural Guidelines and Philosophy](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3439)

- [IANA IP protocol number registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/protocol-numbers/protocol-numbers.xhtml)
- [RFC 9001: QUIC packet and header protection](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001)
- [RFC 7348: VXLAN framing](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7348)

questions.prompt: A receiver's EtherType table maps `0x86DD` to IPv6. An incoming Ethernet frame has that value. What should the receiver do next?

options.text: Pass the entire frame directly to ARP
options.explanation: ARP is a different EtherType; the supplied mapping identifies IPv6.

options.text: Treat the payload as IPv4 because every Ethernet payload is IPv4
options.explanation: Ethernet can carry different protocols, and this frame explicitly selects IPv6.

options.text: Pass the Ethernet payload to IPv6, which interprets its own next-header information
options.explanation: Correct. Selection proceeds one layer at a time; an EtherType does not identify every inner header.

options.text: Pass the payload straight to an HTTPS application
options.explanation: Application delivery requires further IP and transport interpretation; Ethernet does not establish HTTPS merely from this EtherType.

questions.workedExample: Use the supplied mapping to select IPv6. IPv6 then interprets its Next Header field, which may select a transport or an extension header. Transport endpoint information helps select the final recipient. Each layer interprets its own context; port conventions alone do not prove an application protocol.

questions.prompt: An IPv4 packet carrying TCP passes through an ordinary router (no NAT, no firewall). Which of these fields are different when the packet leaves the router compared with when it arrived? Select all that apply. Assume distinct ordinary Ethernet interfaces/next-hop MACs, no IP options, tunnelling or fragmentation, and successful forwarding.

options.text: The Ethernet source and destination MAC addresses
options.explanation: Correct. The router strips the incoming frame and builds a new one for the next link, addressed from its own outgoing interface to the next hop's MAC.

options.text: The IP TTL
options.explanation: Correct. IPv4 forwarding reduces TTL by at least one; expiry prevents indefinite routing loops.

options.text: The IP header checksum
options.explanation: Correct. Because the TTL changed, the IPv4 header checksum must be recomputed (or incrementally updated). IPv6 dropped the header checksum partly to avoid this per-hop work.

options.text: The destination IP address
options.explanation: It stays unchanged under the stated ordinary-forwarding assumptions. Address translation and some routing/tunnelling mechanisms require separate treatment.

options.text: The TCP destination port
options.explanation: The specified plain forwarding operation does not change the TCP destination port. Port rewriting is a NAT behaviour, which this question excludes.

questions.workedExample:
Think about which layers are hop-by-hop and which are end-to-end.

1. **Link layer (hop-by-hop).** Each link gets a brand-new frame. New MACs, new FCS.
2. **Network layer (inspected at every hop).** Addresses stay fixed, but the router decrements TTL. The IPv4 checksum covers the TTL, so it changes too.
3. **Transport and up (end-to-end).** Untouched by a plain router.

So three things change: MACs, TTL and IP checksum. NAT can change an address and optionally a port, requiring checksum correctness to be maintained; not every translation changes every field.

link.title: RFC 1812: Requirements for IP Version 4 Routers

questions.prompt: An ordinary router forwards an IP packet between two Ethernet links. Assume no NAT, tunnel, fragmentation or retransmission. Why does it build a new Ethernet frame?

options.text: The original destination MAC identifies the final server on every routed link
options.explanation: Ethernet addresses identify local link delivery; the final server may be many routed links away.

options.text: Every router must change the IP destination to its own address
options.explanation: Ordinary forwarding preserves the final IP destination under these assumptions.

options.text: The next Ethernet link needs local source and next-hop MAC addresses
options.explanation: Correct. The router terminates incoming link framing and creates framing suitable for its outgoing link.

options.text: TCP ports are different on every Ethernet link
options.explanation: Plain forwarding does not rewrite TCP ports.

questions.workedExample: First separate the boundaries: the IP packet describes delivery across the path; an Ethernet frame describes delivery over the current link or LAN. The router chooses a next hop, then addresses a frame for that next link. IP addresses remain the same here, while TTL and the IPv4 checksum need the appropriate forwarding updates.

lessons.title: Count useful bytes and wire time
lessons.summary: Explain why headers and wire overhead affect small requests more than full frames.
lessons.body:
An application pays for more than its own bytes. Transport, network and link layers add headers, and Ethernet also uses a trailer and time between frames. **Link efficiency** is the share of link occupancy that carries useful data at the boundary you choose.

## A small request and a full frame

Assume a 100-byte HTTP request fits in one TCP segment: no TLS, minimal TCP/IPv4 headers and untagged Ethernet. Ignore acknowledgements, retransmissions and PHY coding.

| Part | Bytes |
|---|---|
| HTTP request | 100 |
| TCP header | 20 |
| IPv4 header | 20 |
| Ethernet header and FCS | 18 |

The resulting frame is 158 bytes from destination MAC to FCS. Ethernet's header contains two 6-byte MAC addresses and a 2-byte EtherType; its **FCS** is a 4-byte CRC trailer.

Wire occupancy also includes an 8-byte preamble/start delimiter and a nominal 12-byte-time **inter-frame gap**. A byte-time is the time to send one byte. The gap is a time allowance, not extra frame payload; the PHY may send idle signalling during it. This request therefore costs 178 byte-times, of which only 100 carry HTTP: about 56% efficiency.

A full 1500-byte IPv4 packet with minimal headers carries 1460 bytes of TCP data and occupies 1538 byte-times under the same accounting. About 95% carries TCP data. The fixed overhead has been spread across much more useful data.

Small messages are still useful: waiting to fill a frame can add latency. The point is to understand the cost, rather than always choose the largest message.

## Count the right boundary

The IP MTU counts the IP packet; Ethernet frame size counts destination MAC through FCS; wire occupancy additionally counts preamble and gap. Confusing these boundaries produces misleading rates.

TCP options use some space inside the same IP MTU, leaving less for data. Tags, encryption and tunnels can add further overhead. A calculated payload ceiling is not a measured application rate: host limits, congestion, acknowledgements and loss can reduce goodput.

## Key takeaways
- Fixed overhead takes a larger share of a small frame's wire time.
- Distinguish useful payload, IP packet size, Ethernet frame size and wire occupancy.

## Further reading
- [RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122)
- [OSI model — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSI_model)
- [Internet protocol suite — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_protocol_suite)
- [Encapsulation (networking) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encapsulation_(networking))
- [RFC 3439: Some Internet Architectural Guidelines and Philosophy](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3439)

- [IANA IP protocol number registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/protocol-numbers/protocol-numbers.xhtml)
- [RFC 9001: QUIC packet and header protection](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001)
- [RFC 7348: VXLAN framing](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7348)

questions.prompt: A capture reports the size of an Ethernet frame from destination MAC through FCS. An engineer treats that byte count as its complete wire-time cost. What is missing under the lesson's nominal framing model?

options.text: The IP header, which is always outside the frame
options.explanation: The IP packet and its header are already inside the Ethernet payload.

options.text: Preamble/start delimiter and the inter-frame gap time
options.explanation: Correct. These consume wire time beyond the counted Ethernet frame; the gap is a time allowance rather than frame payload.

options.text: The FCS, which must be counted twice
options.explanation: The reported boundary already includes the FCS once.

options.text: Nothing: frame length and wire occupancy are identical
options.explanation: That omits the stated framing overhead outside destination-MAC-through-FCS bytes.

questions.workedExample: Identify exactly what the capture counts. The frame contains its header, payload, padding if needed and FCS. Sending consecutive frames also requires preamble/start-delimiter signalling and a nominal gap. A payload-efficiency estimate based only on frame bytes overstates the useful share of wire time.

questions.prompt: A sender adds TCP options while keeping full-size IPv4 packets within the same IP MTU. Assume the same Ethernet wire occupancy per full-size packet. What happens to the ideal TCP payload rate?

options.text: It reaches the full link rate because options are free
options.explanation: Options consume bytes inside the packet; they do not remove Ethernet overhead.

options.text: It increases because a longer TCP header carries more application data
options.explanation: TCP option bytes are control information, not additional application payload.

options.text: It is unchanged because the IP packet length stays fixed
options.explanation: The total length stays fixed, but fewer of those bytes carry TCP data.

options.text: It decreases because option bytes displace TCP data
options.explanation: Correct. With the same full-packet wire-time cost, less useful payload per packet means a lower payload ceiling.

questions.workedExample: Hold the outer budget fixed. The IP header, TCP header and TCP data must fit inside the IP MTU. Enlarging the TCP header leaves less space for data, while the Ethernet frame's total occupancy stays the same in this comparison. Real throughput also depends on the hosts, path and behaviour enabled by the options.

lessons.title: Parse an Ethernet header
lessons.summary: Decode a synthetic header with Python and identify what the limited parser cannot validate.
lessons.body:
### Parsing headers in code

Many header fields have defined byte layouts; optional and variable-length fields need additional parsing. Python's `struct` module can unpack them (`!` means network byte order, which is big-endian):

```python
import struct

def parse_eth(frame: bytes):
    if len(frame) < 14:
        raise ValueError("short header")
    # Decode fixed fields in network order.
    dst, src, etype = struct.unpack(
        "!6s6sH", frame[:14])
    # Keep the payload as uninterpreted
    # bytes.
    return (dst.hex(":"), src.hex(":"),
            hex(etype), frame[14:])

frame = bytes.fromhex(
    "ffffffffffff" "3c22fb112233"
    "0806") + b"..."

# Show addresses and ARP protocol selection.
print(parse_eth(frame)[:3])
# ('ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff',
#  '3c:22:fb:11:22:33', '0x806')
```

The tuple contains the destination, source and EtherType. The final return value is the bytes after the fixed header; the displayed slice deliberately omits it. The length check rejects an incomplete fixed header before `struct.unpack` reads it.

This is a synthetic header followed by placeholder bytes, not a valid complete ARP frame. Its all-ones destination denotes broadcast and its EtherType selects ARP, which you will meet in the ARP units. This parser demonstrates an untagged Ethernet II header only. It does not handle VLAN tags, 802.3 length/LLC framing, frame length validation or FCS stripping/verification; packet-capture APIs may omit the FCS.

## Key takeaways
- Network byte order puts the most significant byte first.
- Parsing 14 header bytes does not validate the whole frame or its FCS.

## Further reading
- [RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts — Communication Layers](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc1122)
- [OSI model — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSI_model)
- [Internet protocol suite — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_protocol_suite)
- [Encapsulation (networking) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encapsulation_(networking))
- [RFC 3439: Some Internet Architectural Guidelines and Philosophy](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3439)

- [IANA IP protocol number registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/protocol-numbers/protocol-numbers.xhtml)
- [RFC 9001: QUIC packet and header protection](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9001)
- [RFC 7348: VXLAN framing](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7348)

questions.prompt: The lesson’s parser accepts a 14-byte Ethernet header followed by three placeholder bytes. What has this successfully checked?

options.text: Only that enough fixed-header bytes exist to unpack
options.explanation: Correct. The length guard checks 14 bytes; it does not validate a full frame, payload or FCS.

options.text: That the ARP payload is valid
options.explanation: EtherType selects a protocol, but the payload is returned without parsing.

options.text: That the frame passes its CRC
options.explanation: The parser never computes or verifies an FCS.

options.text: That every VLAN tag has been decoded
options.explanation: The limited parser treats the fixed field as EtherType and does not parse VLAN tags.

questions.workedExample:
1. The length guard requires at least 14 bytes.
2. `struct.unpack` reads the fixed destination, source and type fields.
3. Remaining bytes are returned untouched.
4. Therefore successful unpacking proves neither valid ARP nor a complete Ethernet frame.

lessons.title: Where network layers interact
lessons.summary: Recognise checksum, NAT, MTU and middlebox interactions across layer boundaries.
lessons.body:
## Why layering works

- **Independent evolution.** A faster Ethernet link does not inherently require a new TCP wire format. An application protocol can evolve without redesigning link framing.
- **Interchangeable parts.** IP runs over Ethernet, Wi-Fi, 5G, satellite and (famously, in RFC 1149) carrier pigeons. Anything that can carry a packet can be part of the internet.
- **The narrow waist.** Many link technologies below and many applications above all meet at a single network protocol, IP. IP is the common internetworking service in this model; applications normally use higher-level APIs, while lower-layer devices need not implement an IP endpoint.
- **Each device does only what it needs.** Basic bridging uses link-layer information, while IP routing uses network-layer information. Real switches and routers can also inspect higher layers for filtering, load distribution or other functions.

## Where layering leaks

In theory a layer knows nothing about the others. In practice the boundaries leak, and many real problems live in those leaks.

- **TCP checksums cover IP addresses.** The TCP checksum includes a "pseudo-header" of source and destination IP. So address translation must preserve checksum correctness by adjusting or recomputing it; particular changes can cancel numerically.
- **Address/port translation.** A home gateway can use network address and port translation to share a public address. It may preserve a source port when possible or rewrite it when required by its mapping policy.
- **MTU.** The network layer needs the link MTU: the maximum network-layer packet that fits, rather than the whole Ethernet frame including its header and FCS. An oversized packet may be fragmented when permitted, or rejected with an ICMP message. If the required signalling or discovery fails, a path-MTU black hole can make larger traffic fail while smaller packets work.
- **Middleboxes inspect layer 4.** Firewalls and load balancers parse TCP headers and drop what they do not recognise. Such **ossification** can impede new transports and extensions. QUIC uses UDP to improve deployability and protects packet contents and selected header fields to limit unwanted dependencies; some headers remain visible and some networks block UDP or QUIC.
- **Wireless loss looks like congestion.** Loss-based TCP congestion control treats loss as a congestion signal, even when a particular loss comes from corruption rather than queue overflow. Reducing the rate may not address that radio error, and link-layer retransmissions can recover some radio loss before TCP sees it. Wi-Fi retry mechanisms also benefit other traffic; TCP is not their sole reason for existing.
- **Layers that do not fit.** MPLS is often called "layer 2.5". TLS sits between transport and application. Some tunnels, such as VXLAN, carry an inner Ethernet frame inside UDP (without the original FCS); other VPNs tunnel IP packets or application data instead.

> [!note] Layering is a model, not a law
> Treat the layers as a way to reason about responsibilities. Expect real systems to cross them for performance, security or historical reasons, and expect bugs where they do.

## Key takeaways
- Layering allows independent evolution but practical boundaries can interact.
- NAT, MTU discovery, encrypted transports and tunnels need coordinated accounting.

## Further reading

- [OSI model — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OSI_model)
- [Internet protocol suite — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_protocol_suite)
- [Encapsulation (networking) — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Encapsulation_(networking))

- [IANA IP protocol number registry](https://www.iana.org/assignments/protocol-numbers/protocol-numbers.xhtml)

questions.prompt: A home NAT router rewrites a packet's source IP from 192.168.1.20 to its public address, and its source port too. Why must it also update the **TCP** checksum, even though the TCP payload hasn't changed?

options.text: Because the TCP checksum covers a pseudo-header that includes the source and destination IP addresses, as well as the TCP header with its ports
options.explanation: Correct. Addresses and TCP ports are checksum inputs, so translation must maintain the checksum by adjustment or recomputation. Some numerical changes can cancel, leaving the checksum value unchanged.

options.text: Because the TTL changed and TCP checksums cover the TTL
options.explanation: The TTL is not part of the TCP pseudo-header. The TTL change only affects the IPv4 header checksum.

options.text: It doesn't need to; TCP checksums only cover TCP data
options.explanation: TCP includes a pseudo-header and its own header as well as data. Ignoring changed checksum inputs can cause validation failure.

options.text: Because the Ethernet FCS is copied into the TCP header
options.explanation: The FCS is a link-layer trailer recomputed on every hop. It is never copied into TCP.

questions.workedExample: TCP covers its IP pseudo-header, TCP header and data. Translation changes some of these inputs. The translator must maintain a valid checksum, usually through incremental adjustment or recomputation. It need not become numerically different for every possible pair of changes.

questions.prompt: Why does QUIC run over UDP rather than being a new transport protocol with its own IP protocol number, alongside TCP (6) and UDP (17)?

options.text: Because UDP provides the reliability that QUIC needs
options.explanation: UDP provides no reliability at all. QUIC implements its own acknowledgements, retransmission and congestion control on top.

options.text: Because IP has no spare protocol numbers left
options.explanation: IP protocol numbers are not exhausted. The relevant concern is support by deployed networks and endpoints.

options.text: UDP improves deployability through existing endpoint APIs and many NATs and firewalls compared with an unfamiliar IP transport protocol
options.explanation: Correct. This is not universal reachability: some networks block UDP or QUIC. QUIC protects packet contents and selected header fields; it does not encrypt every header field.

options.text: Because the operating system kernel can only send TCP or UDP
options.explanation: Kernels can send arbitrary IP protocols (SCTP exists, for example). Being in user space is a bonus of UDP, but the main reason is what the network lets through.

questions.workedExample: A new IP transport number can require middlebox and endpoint support. UDP provides an already supported transport substrate in many environments, making deployment easier. QUIC adds transport and security functionality above UDP. Its protected contents and selected protected header fields reduce some ossification risks, while fields such as connection IDs remain visible. Neither UDP reachability nor freedom from ossification is guaranteed.

questions.prompt: A VXLAN tunnel must fit an inner Ethernet frame inside UDP and an outer IP packet. The underlay's IP MTU is unchanged. Why can a tenant's previously valid full-size IP packet become too large?

options.text: The tunnel headers use no space inside the outer IP packet
options.explanation: Outer IP, UDP and VXLAN headers occupy part of that packet budget.

options.text: Only the outer Ethernet FCS reduces the outer IP MTU
options.explanation: The outer Ethernet header and FCS sit outside the outer IP packet's MTU budget.

options.text: Tunnel headers and the inner Ethernet header consume part of the outer IP-packet budget
options.explanation: Correct. The tenant's IP packet shares that outer budget with encapsulation that was absent before.

options.text: The tenant's TCP port number gets wider inside VXLAN
options.explanation: VXLAN encapsulates the frame; it does not widen transport port fields.

questions.workedExample: Draw the nesting: outer Ethernet contains outer IP, which contains UDP, VXLAN and the inner Ethernet frame. The underlay IP MTU limits the entire outer IP packet. The tenant's IP packet is only part of that budget. Check a sufficient underlay MTU or reduce the tenant MTU; unresolved fragmentation or path-MTU adaptation can otherwise cause size-dependent failure.

link.title: RFC 7348: Virtual eXtensible Local Area Network (VXLAN)

questions.prompt: Which examples show interaction across layers or an intermediate system processing higher-layer information? Select all that apply.

options.text: Wi-Fi link retries can recover radio losses before TCP sees them and responds with congestion control
options.explanation: Correct. This is a cross-layer performance interaction, but retries also serve other protocols and do not exist solely because of TCP.

options.text: A load balancer reads the HTTP Host header to choose a backend
options.explanation: Correct. An application proxy processes layer-7 information. That does not itself prove ossification or violate the layering model.

options.text: The IP layer needs to know the link's MTU to size its packets
options.explanation: Correct. MTU is a link service property used by IP. Depending on IP version and policy, an oversized packet can be fragmented, rejected or dropped; such an interface is not inherently a design flaw.

options.text: HTTP/2 was deployed without any changes to Ethernet
options.explanation: That's the opposite: layering *working* as intended. Ethernet carries whatever payload it is given.

lessons.title: Rate, units and transmission time
lessons.summary: Distinguish link capacity from latency and predict how packet size and link rate affect transmission.
lessons.body:
A connection can move a lot of data each second yet respond slowly. Buying more bandwidth helps when capacity is the constraint; it cannot make a signal travel a fixed route faster.

## Bandwidth and latency

**Bandwidth**, also called link rate or capacity here, is how many bits a link can put onto the medium per second. **Latency** is the time a bit or packet takes to reach its destination, using the timing boundary specified.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: More lanes
> Adding lanes to a road lets more vehicles travel at once. It does not shorten the route.
>
> **How it maps:** Link capacity is like the number of lanes; propagation time is like the journey along the route. More capacity can reduce congestion and the time needed to send a whole packet.
>
> **Where it stops:** Packets are serialised into signals, and routers add processing and queueing. A road journey does not model all those delays.

> [!warning] Bits and bytes
> Network rates use decimal SI units and bits: 1 Mbit/s is 1,000,000 bits per second. One byte is 8 bits. File sizes may use decimal bytes (MB) or binary units (KiB, with 1024 bytes per KiB). A 100 Mbit/s link has an ideal ceiling of 12.5 MB/s before overhead; a browser's displayed rate requires measurement.

## Transmission delay

Transmission delay is the time to put all of one packet's bits onto the link, from its first bit to its last. Larger packets take longer. A higher link rate sends the same packet in less time. Cable length plays no part in this particular delay.

```formula reference
d_trans = L / R
where
d_trans: transmission delay, in seconds, from putting the first packet bit onto the link to putting the last bit onto it
L: packet length in bits, counted at the layer being modelled
R: link rate in bits per second
In words: transmission takes longer for a larger packet and less time on a higher-rate link; doubling both packet size and link rate leaves this delay unchanged.
```

For example, putting a 1500-byte packet onto a 100 Mbit/s link takes 120 microseconds, ignoring additional framing and encoding. At 1 Gbit/s it takes 12 microseconds. The signal still needs time to travel after the first bit enters the medium.

Overhead, server work, congestion and host limits can make a file transfer slower than the raw rate suggests. Keep the units and the measured boundary explicit.

## Key takeaways
- Capacity describes a rate; latency describes a time.
- Packet size and link rate determine transmission delay; route length determines a different delay.

lessons.title: Distance and propagation delay
lessons.summary: Explain the propagation floor and distinguish route length from link rate.
lessons.body:
Propagation delay is how long a signal takes to travel through the medium. A longer route takes longer; a medium with a higher signal speed takes less time.

## Distance sets a floor

In this model, propagation depends on route length and signal speed, rather than packet size or bit rate. Increasing the rate alone puts bits onto the link faster but does not make each bit travel faster.

```formula reference
d_prop = d / v
where
d_prop: one-way propagation delay in seconds
d: length of the signal's route in metres
v: signal speed in the medium in metres per second; roughly 200 million in ordinary solid-glass fibre and close to 300 million for radio in air
In words: propagation time grows with distance and falls with signal speed; halving the route length halves this delay.
```

A useful teaching approximation for ordinary solid-glass fibre is about 5 microseconds per kilometre, or 1 millisecond per 200 km. The precise value depends on fibre construction and wavelength; some cables also have different speeds.

For a hypothetical 5,600 km fibre route at 200,000 km/s, propagation takes 28 ms each way. If the return follows the same route and speed, propagation alone contributes 56 ms to the round-trip time (**RTT**, there and back). Processing, transmission and queueing add more.

These are specified-model results, not measured city-pair latencies. A real route may be longer than the distance on a map.

## What can improve it?

A shorter route or a faster propagation medium can reduce propagation delay. Radio in air travels faster than light in typical solid-glass fibre, but a real radio link has its own capacity, reliability and equipment constraints.

A higher bit rate or smaller packet can reduce transmission delay while leaving propagation unchanged. An upgrade that also changes the route, wavelength or medium may change both; identify which property actually changed.

## Key takeaways
- Propagation follows route length and signal speed.
- A faster link rate alone leaves propagation time unchanged.

lessons.title: Combine the four delays
lessons.summary: Diagnose four delay components and explain store-and-forward packet pipelining.
lessons.body:
A packet can be delayed before transmission, during transmission, while travelling, and while a device examines it. Separating these costs helps identify which change could improve a slow path.

## Four contributions

- **Queueing:** waiting behind traffic that shares the output link. An idle link can have no queueing delay; a congested one can add hundreds of milliseconds.
- **Transmission:** putting every packet bit onto the link. Packet size and link rate determine this.
- **Propagation:** the signal travelling along the route. Distance and medium determine this.
- **Processing:** examining headers, checking errors and deciding what to do. Hardware, software, enabled features and load affect the time.

Variation in packet delay is commonly called **jitter**. Queueing contributes to jitter, but is not its only possible source.

To model one hop, add the relevant waiting, transmission, propagation and processing times. For a whole path, account for each link and each device once at the chosen timing boundary.

## Store-and-forward and pipelining

With **store-and-forward**, a device receives the complete packet before sending it onward. One packet crossing two such links therefore pays a transmission delay on each link. **Cut-through** forwarding can overlap reception with onward transmission and needs a different model.

For a concrete two-link example, assume a 1500-byte packet, two 100 Mbit/s links spanning 200 km and 800 km, one router taking 20 microseconds, no queues and no framing overhead. At the assumed 5 microseconds per kilometre, propagation contributes 5 ms; both transmissions and processing together contribute 0.26 ms. The total is about 5.26 ms. Increasing link rate addresses only part of this example's delay.

Splitting a message into packets lets different links work on different packets simultaneously. On equal-rate, initially idle links, later packets can follow the first one at one packet-transmission interval apart. For this illustration, ignore propagation and processing; each row is one packet-transmission interval:

| Interval | Link 1 | Link 2 | Link 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| First | P1 | — | — |
| Second | P2 | P1 | — |
| Third | P3 | P2 | P1 |
| Fourth | — | P3 | P2 |
| Fifth | — | — | P3 |

Each router still receives a whole packet before forwarding it; work overlaps across links. Two packets do not transmit simultaneously on the same serial link. Extra per-packet headers are excluded from this illustration: splitting too finely can waste capacity.

## Key takeaways
- Different delay components respond to different improvements.
- Store-and-forward repeats transmission per link; packet pipelining overlaps work across links.

lessons.title: Why busy queues become slow
lessons.summary: Explain why queues grow near capacity and why high throughput can hide bufferbloat.
lessons.body:
A link with spare capacity on average can still build queues. Bursts temporarily arrive faster than the link can serve them; spare capacity between bursts is what lets that backlog drain.

## Why delay grows near full load

**Traffic intensity**, often called utilisation in the simple model, compares the average incoming work with the link's service capacity. Traffic asking for 90 Mbit/s on a 100 Mbit/s link represents 90% load.

With sustained offered work above service capacity, an ideal infinite queue has no stable finite backlog. A real finite buffer eventually fills and drops or rejects excess traffic. Below capacity, the average load alone still does not determine delay: burstiness, packet sizes, scheduling and competing traffic matter.

Near full load there is little spare service capacity to drain bursts. A small rise in average traffic can therefore produce a much larger rise in waiting time.

## An illustrative queue model

The **M/M/1 queue** makes this effect precise under particular assumptions: Poisson arrivals (independent random arrivals at a steady average rate), independent exponentially distributed service times, one server, infinite waiting space and offered load below capacity.

In that model the mean queueing wait is one mean packet-service time at 50% load, four at 80%, nine at 90% and 99 at 99%. Delay grows much faster than the offered load near capacity. The mean is finite below full load under these assumptions.

```formula reference
W_q = (ρ / (1 − ρ)) T_s
where
W_q: mean time spent waiting before transmission starts, in seconds
ρ: traffic intensity, the average arriving work divided by service capacity; a unitless fraction between zero and one, strictly below one for this model
T_s: mean service time, the average transmission time of a packet, in seconds
In words: in this particular random-arrival, random-service queue model, waiting grows sharply as offered work approaches service capacity because less spare capacity remains to clear bursts.
```

Fixed-size packets have fixed transmission times rather than exponential ones. Real arrival patterns and schedulers also differ. This model is neither a universal prediction nor a bound for routers.

## Bufferbloat

Very large buffers can keep throughput high while allowing hundreds of milliseconds of persistent queueing. This **bufferbloat** hurts calls and games during a bulk upload. Active queue management, including CoDel and FQ-CoDel, addresses persistent queues; FQ-CoDel also separates traffic into flow queues.

Measure latency under load as well as throughput. An impressive bulk-transfer rate does not establish that interactive traffic is responsive.

## Key takeaways
- Average spare capacity does not prevent transient queues.
- Near capacity, waiting can grow sharply; exact values depend on the queue model.
- Throughput and latency under load reveal different aspects of a link.

lessons.title: Data in flight and window limits
lessons.summary: Explain why long, high-capacity paths need more data in flight and can be window-limited.
lessons.body:
A sender learns that data arrived only when an acknowledgement (**ACK**) returns. A high-capacity path with a long round trip can therefore hold a lot of sent-but-unacknowledged data.

## Keeping enough data in flight

To sustain a target payload rate, a steady sender needs permission to keep roughly a round trip's worth of payload in flight. This is the **bandwidth-delay product**. A higher target rate or longer acknowledgement round-trip time increases the required flight allowance.

```formula reference
BDP = R RTT
where
BDP: bandwidth-delay product, the target amount of unacknowledged payload in bits
R: target payload rate in bits per second
RTT: acknowledgement round-trip time in seconds, from sending data until its acknowledgement returns
In words: sustaining a higher payload rate or waiting longer for feedback requires more data in flight; doubling either doubles the steady flight-size target.
```

At a hypothetical 1 Gbit/s payload rate and 70 ms acknowledgement RTT, about 8.75 MB would be unacknowledged. This is a payload target, not a universal socket-memory setting: actual operating-system buffer accounting differs.

## A window can be the bottleneck

The **TCP send window** limits how much data may remain unacknowledged. If it is too small for the target rate and RTT, the sender must wait even when the path has spare capacity.

ACKs can advance a sliding window continuously; the sender need not stop after each batch. Nevertheless, in a steady window-limited model, its delivered rate is bounded by about one window's worth per round trip.

```formula reference
X ≤ W / RTT
where
X: steady payload throughput in bits per second
W: the active allowance for unacknowledged payload in bits
RTT: acknowledgement round-trip time in seconds
≤: less than or equal to; this is an upper bound rather than a throughput prediction
In words: a fixed flight allowance supports less throughput when acknowledgements take longer to return, even if link capacity is plentiful.
```

Without negotiated **window scaling**, TCP's 16-bit receive-window field represents at most 65,535 bytes. If this is the active limit over a 70 ms RTT, it caps steady payload throughput near 7.5 Mbit/s. Window scaling allows larger advertised receive windows when negotiated; sender congestion limits, receiver space and other constraints still apply.

Paths with large bandwidth-delay products are called **long fat networks**. They need adequate flight allowances, appropriate buffering and recovery that handles many packets in flight. Simply increasing a physical link's rate may leave the limiting window unchanged.

## Key takeaways
- Higher target rates and longer feedback delays need more payload in flight.
- A small active window can limit throughput despite spare link capacity.
- Window scaling increases representable receive windows; it does not remove all throughput limits.

lessons.title: Throughput and useful goodput
lessons.summary: Separate bottleneck capacity, achieved throughput and useful payload goodput.
lessons.body:
A link's nominal capacity, the traffic it actually carries, and the useful data delivered to an application are different measurements.

## The bottleneck sets a ceiling

**Throughput** is the rate actually achieved at a stated boundary. A path cannot carry traffic faster than its slowest link, the **bottleneck**. A 1 Gbit/s home LAN behind a 100 Mbit/s broadband link can reach the internet at no more than 100 Mbit/s through that route.

Competition with other flows, active window limits, host performance and congestion can make the achieved rate lower still. A bottleneck capacity is a ceiling, not a promised result.

## Goodput counts useful data once

**Goodput** counts useful application data delivered per second. It excludes headers, duplicate transmission attempts, pure acknowledgements and handshakes. State the boundary: TCP payload rate can still include TLS or application-protocol overhead that file goodput excludes.

For the earlier one-direction, untagged full-duplex Ethernet model, a 1500-byte IPv4 packet with minimal TCP/IP headers carries 1460 bytes of TCP payload in 1538 byte-times of wire occupancy. On 1 Gbit/s Ethernet that allows about 949 Mbit/s of TCP payload. Twelve bytes of TCP options lower it to about 941 Mbit/s.

These are ideal framing ceilings. They assume hosts, acknowledgement handling, congestion and loss do not constrain the rate, and exclude additional application/TLS overhead.

## What retransmissions change

A retransmission may finally deliver data that was lost, but delivering that payload then consumed more than one attempt. Goodput counts the useful payload once.

In a saturated-link accounting model with equal payload sizes and 2% of attempts being extra retransmissions, useful rate falls by another 2% after framing overhead. Real loss can additionally trigger congestion control, idle time or timeouts, so this accounting is not a general loss-to-throughput prediction.

When a transfer is slow, measure the bottleneck, retries, window limits and host work. A higher line-rate label alone does not explain the outcome.

## Key takeaways
- Bottleneck capacity bounds throughput; other constraints can reduce it further.
- Goodput excludes overhead and counts useful delivered bytes only once.
- Retransmission accounting alone does not predict TCP's congestion response.

lessons.title: Optimise small and large transfers
lessons.summary: Choose between reducing round trips and increasing sustained goodput for different workloads.
lessons.body:
Small exchanges are often dominated by round trips; sufficiently large transfers can be dominated by sustained goodput. Server work, congestion and host performance can dominate either, so diagnose the workload first.

## Compare two workloads

Assume a hypothetical path with a 100 Mbit/s payload rate and a 40 ms round-trip time. Ignore DNS, server work, loss, slow start and additional overhead. Use fresh TCP plus a full TLS 1.3 handshake with no resumption, early data or retry.

- A **20 KB API response** waits through TCP setup, TLS setup and the request/response round trip. Those three round trips cost about 120 ms, while response transmission takes only about 1.6 ms.
- A **1 GB download** needs about 80 seconds of payload transmission. The same setup cost is small beside that.

Sending the small response at a higher payload rate removes little of its delay. Reducing RTT or avoiding repeated setup addresses the larger cost in this model. For the large download, improving sustained goodput can make a substantial difference.

## Avoid unnecessary round trips

Connection reuse avoids repeating setup for every request. A server location with a lower measured RTT shortens each required round trip.

A conventional full TLS 1.2 handshake without resumption or False Start takes two TLS round trips before the request. With one TCP setup round trip and one request/response round trip, that simplified fresh-connection model needs four RTTs. TLS 1.3 reduces the TLS part to one unless retry adds another exchange.

TLS/QUIC early data (**0-RTT**) requires prior connection state and replay-safe application handling. It is not available for every first connection, and replay risk matters when a request changes state.

These examples isolate mechanisms. Real workloads can involve parallel requests, caching, congestion, server computation and connection limits. There is no universal bandwidth threshold beyond which pages stop benefiting.

## Key takeaways
- Small exchanges can benefit most from fewer or shorter round trips.
- Large transfers can benefit most from higher sustained goodput.
- Reuse and handshake choices depend on protocol and application constraints.

lessons.title: Symbols, baud and bits
lessons.summary: Distinguish symbol rate from bit rate and explain why denser signalling needs reliable distinction.
lessons.body:
The physical layer turns bits into signals that travel as voltages, light or radio waves. It chooses from distinguishable **symbols**, such as voltage levels or combinations of amplitude and phase.

## Symbols and bits measure different things

The **baud rate** counts symbols per second. The **bit rate** also depends on how much information each symbol distinguishes.

With two states, one symbol can distinguish 0 from 1. With four states it can distinguish 00, 01, 10 and 11: two bits per symbol. Each extra bit requires twice as many states for an uncoded fixed mapping.

| Scheme | States | Bits per symbol |
|---|---|---|
| Two voltage levels | 2 | 1 |
| PAM-4 | 4 | 2 |
| 16-QAM | 16 | 4 |
| 1024-QAM, used in Wi-Fi 6 | 1024 | 10 |

A 1 Gbaud PAM-4 mapping therefore represents 2 Gbit/s before overhead. Coding, framing and pilots (known reference symbols used by the receiver) reduce the useful payload rate.

```formula reference
k = log_2(M)
R_b = R_s k
where
k: number of bits carried by each symbol in the uncoded fixed mapping
M: number of distinguishable symbol states; assume a power of two for the fixed whole-bit mapping
log_2: base-two logarithm, the power to which two must be raised to obtain the argument
R_b: raw mapped bit rate in bits per second
R_s: symbol rate in symbols per second, also called baud
In words: more symbol states let each symbol carry more bits, and sending more symbols each second raises the raw bit rate; coding and other overhead reduce the useful payload rate.
```

## Why more levels have a cost

At a fixed signal range, putting states closer together makes them harder to distinguish in noise. More states can raise bits per symbol while also making the mapping less robust.

A receiver also needs suitable pulse shaping and timing: the waveform need not stay constant during a symbol interval. Choosing modulation means balancing rate against the channel conditions, coding and implementation limits.

## Key takeaways
- Baud counts symbols; bit rate also counts the bits represented by each symbol.
- Denser signal states increase raw rate but require reliable distinction in noise.

lessons.title: The ideal Nyquist limit
lessons.summary: Explain the ideal symbol-rate limit, bandwidth conventions and limits of adding levels.
lessons.body:
A physical channel passes a limited range of frequencies. Here **bandwidth** means that frequency range in hertz, rather than a network's advertised bit rate.

## Symbols must remain distinguishable

Pulses can spread into neighbouring symbol intervals, causing **intersymbol interference**. Ideal pulse shaping can arrange for neighbouring pulses to contribute zero at the receiver's sampling instants.

For a noiseless real low-pass channel, one-sided bandwidth is measured from zero frequency to the upper limit. The ideal Nyquist zero-intersymbol-interference model supports a maximum real symbol rate of twice that bandwidth. This is a model with particular bandwidth and signalling conventions, not a universal factor to apply to every radio rate.

More distinguishable levels allow more bits in each symbol. Four levels carry two bits per symbol; increasing the number of levels does not increase bits per symbol in direct proportion.

```formula reference
C = 2B log_2(M)
where
C: maximum uncoded bit rate in the stated noiseless real-baseband model, in bits per second
B: one-sided low-pass bandwidth in hertz, measured from zero frequency to the upper limit
M: number of distinguishable signal levels; a power of two for a fixed whole-bit mapping
log_2: base-two logarithm; it gives bits per symbol for this mapping
In words: the stated ideal model limits the symbol rate through bandwidth, while the number of distinguishable levels determines how many bits each symbol carries.
```

For example, a hypothetical noiseless 3.1 kHz baseband channel with four levels permits 6,200 real symbols per second, each carrying two bits, for 12.4 kbit/s. These values illustrate the assumptions; finite implementations and overhead require separate accounting.

## Noise changes the problem

The noiseless model does not decide how many closely spaced levels a real receiver can reliably distinguish. Noise can blur them together. Shannon's noisy-channel limit addresses that additional constraint.

Increasing the number of levels on an unchanged noisy channel therefore does not guarantee a usable rate increase. Both bandwidth and reliable distinction matter.

## Key takeaways
- The Nyquist zero-ISI model constrains real symbol rate for its stated one-sided baseband bandwidth.
- More levels carry more bits per symbol, but noise constrains usable signalling.

lessons.title: Noise, SNR and Shannon capacity
lessons.summary: Explain noisy-channel capacity, decibel power ratios and bandwidth-versus-power trade-offs.
lessons.body:
A receiver must distinguish signal from noise. Choosing more modulation states cannot create unlimited reliable capacity when noise blurs those states.

## A limit for a specified noisy channel

For a band-limited **additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN)** channel, noise is modelled as random Gaussian variation added to the signal, with equal average noise power in equal-width frequency bands across the channel. Shannon capacity gives the highest reliable information rate in this model under its average-power constraint.

At rates below capacity, suitable coding can make error probability arbitrarily small as coding length grows. This is not a promise of zero errors for finite packets.

```formula reference
C = B log_2(1 + S / N)
where
C: Shannon capacity of the stated AWGN model, in bits per second
B: channel bandwidth in hertz
S: average received signal power in watts
N: average noise power in the channel bandwidth, in watts
log_2: base-two logarithm
In words: holding the signal-to-noise power ratio fixed, more bandwidth raises capacity in direct proportion; at high signal-to-noise ratios, increasing signal power gives progressively smaller proportional gains.
```

The **signal-to-noise ratio (SNR)** compares signal power with noise power. Engineers often express it in **decibels (dB)**: every additional 10 dB multiplies the power ratio by ten. Thus 30 dB represents a signal power 1000 times the noise power. A dB value is not itself the power ratio.

```formula reference
SNR_dB = 10 log_10(S / N)
S / N = 10^(SNR_dB / 10)
where
SNR_dB: signal-to-noise ratio in decibels
S: signal power in watts
N: noise power in watts, measured over the same channel
log_10: base-ten logarithm
In words: decibels describe a power ratio logarithmically; an increase of ten decibels means ten times the ratio, rather than ten more units of signal power.
```

## What can improve capacity?

For a hypothetical single flat AWGN channel, 20 MHz at 30 dB SNR has about 199 Mbit/s capacity. At the same SNR, doubling bandwidth doubles capacity. Doubling signal power while holding noise and bandwidth fixed gives a much smaller proportional improvement at this high SNR.

Keeping SNR fixed while widening a channel is an explicit assumption. If total signal power stays fixed and noise spectral density stays constant, a wider channel admits more noise and reduces SNR.

Actual Wi-Fi systems also involve multiple spatial channels, contention, pilots, coding and protocol overhead. Independent spatial channels can add capacity, but simply adding antennas does not guarantee independence. Attenuation, interference, propagation paths and equipment affect achievable rates.

## Key takeaways
- Capacity depends on channel bandwidth and signal-to-noise power ratio.
- More modulation levels cannot defeat the stated channel limit.
- The asymptotic theorem does not promise error-free finite packets or model a complete Wi-Fi network.

lessons.title: Line codes and clock recovery
lessons.summary: Trace clock-recovery coding and explain why coded line bits exceed payload bits.
lessons.body:
## Line coding: why not just send the bits?

The simplest scheme, **NRZ** (non-return-to-zero), maps 1 to high and 0 to low. It has two problems:

1. **Clock recovery.** Assume the receiver has no separate clock and must recover timing from the data. It finds bit boundaries by watching for transitions. A sufficiently long transition-free run can exceed the receiver’s clock-recovery tolerance; not every finite run necessarily causes an error.
2. **Baseline wander (DC balance).** Many links are AC-coupled through electrical transformers or capacitors. A long run of 1s looks like a constant DC level, which the coupling blocks, so the receiver's idea of "zero" drifts.

**Line coding and scrambling** address transition density and baseline wander, but different schemes provide different guarantees.

**Manchester** coding (used by 10 Mbit/s Ethernet) puts a transition in the middle of every bit. In IEEE 802.3's convention, 0 is high-to-low and 1 is low-to-high:

```
bit:        1    0    1    1
NRZ:        HH   LL   HH   HH
Manchester: LH   HL   LH   LH
```

```python
def manchester(bits):
    # IEEE 802.3: 0 -> high,low
    #             1 -> low,high
    out = []
    # Expand each bit into two half-bit
    # levels.
    for b in bits:
        if b not in "01":
            raise ValueError("not binary")
        if b == "1":
            out += [0, 1]
        else:
            out += [1, 0]
    return out


# Each adjacent pair represents one bit.
print(manchester("1011"))
# [0, 1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0, 1]
```

Manchester is self-clocking and DC-balanced, but it **doubles the signalling rate**: two half-bit signal levels per bit. Other Ethernet PHYs use different tradeoffs.

Some faster links use **block codes**, sometimes combined with scrambling and a separate line modulation. They provide different transition-density and DC-balance guarantees:

| Code | Used by | Overhead |
|---|---|---|
| 4B/5B | 100BASE-TX, FDDI | 25% |
| 8b/10b | 1000BASE-X, SATA, PCIe 1–2 | 25% |
| 64b/66b | 10GBASE-R | 3.125% |

The name says how many line bits replace how many data bits: 8b/10b sends 10 bits on the line for every 8 bits of data. The coded-bit rate must therefore exceed the uncoded data-bit rate.

For example, 10 Gbit/s of data with 64b/66b coding needs 10.3125 Gbit/s of coded line bits. Those additional bits support the code; they are not extra application payload.

Specifically, 100BASE-TX maps its 4B/5B-coded stream to MLT-3 at 125 million symbol intervals/s. Serial binary 10GBASE-R uses 10.3125 Gbaud. Other Fast/Gigabit Ethernet PHYs need not use those rates. Good line codes also leave unused code words that can be used for control, such as marking the start of a frame.

## Key takeaways
- Clock recovery and baseline stability need suitable transition and balance properties.
- Different block codes and scramblers provide different guarantees and overheads.

lessons.title: Copper and wireless trade-offs
lessons.summary: Compare differential copper signalling with shared, fading radio channels.
lessons.body:
## Copper

**Twisted pair** (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a) is the familiar Ethernet cable. Each pair carries a signal as a voltage *difference* between two wires. Twisting them means external interference hits both wires almost equally, and the receiver, looking only at the difference, rejects its common-mode component to the extent allowed by cable balance and receiver performance. Twisting also reduces **crosstalk** between neighbouring pairs.

- Common four-pair building-cabling Ethernet standards support **100 m** channels with the required cable category and installation quality. Other Ethernet PHYs and products have different reach limits. Signals attenuate and pick up noise with length, and higher frequencies attenuate faster.
- **1000BASE-T** sends PAM-5 on all four pairs at 125 Mbaud, in both directions at once, using echo cancellation to separate its own transmit signal from the incoming one.
- **10GBASE-T** can support 100 m on compliant Cat6a channels with suitable endpoints. Reach on other cable categories and power relative to optical alternatives require the specific cable and transceiver specifications; universal figures are omitted.
- **Coaxial cable** (a centre conductor in a shield) carried early Ethernet and still carries cable broadband (DOCSIS).

## Wireless

Radio has no cable at all, which brings great convenience and a long list of problems:

- **Shared medium.** Devices share radio resources, but hidden nodes, distance and obstacles mean not every transmitter can hear every other. Transmissions collide and must be coordinated (Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CA, covered in a later module).
- **Attenuation.** For the far-field free-space model with fixed transmit power, frequency and antenna gains, received power scales as inverse distance squared: doubling the distance quarters the power, a drop of about 6 dB (since 3 dB is a factor of 2, 6 dB is a factor of 4). Walls, antenna patterns, regulations and multipath alter actual coverage. Higher frequency is not by itself a universal range guarantee.
- **Multipath.** Signals bounce off walls and arrive several times with different delays, interfering with each other. OFDM (splitting a channel into many narrow subcarriers) and MIMO make multipath manageable, even useful.
- **Variable SNR.** Moving a few metres can change SNR a lot, so Wi-Fi and 4G/5G constantly adapt their modulation: higher-order modulation when conditions permit, more robust modulation/coding when needed; distance alone does not determine the mode.
- **Half duplex.** A radio cannot easily hear a faint incoming signal while it transmits a strong one on the same frequency, so it generally takes turns. This is also why Wi-Fi cannot detect collisions the way early Ethernet did.
- **High error rates.** Wireless errors depend on interference, fading and link design. Many systems use error correction and link retries; not every wireless frame is acknowledged, and no universal wired/wireless loss ratio is given here.

## Comparing the media

| Medium | Typical reach | Signal speed |
|---|---|---|
| Four-pair building Ethernet | often 100 m | cable-specific |
| OM3/OM4 with 10GBASE-SR | 300/400 m | fibre-specific |
| Single-mode with 10GBASE-LR | 10 km | fibre-specific |
| Radio (Wi-Fi) | installation-specific | ~c |

## Key takeaways
- Twisted pairs reject common-mode interference within practical balance limits.
- Radio rate and reliability depend on interference, fading, coordination and adaptation.

questions.prompt: Which of these statements about twisted-pair Ethernet cabling are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The receiver measures the voltage difference between the two wires of a pair, so interference that affects both wires equally cancels out
options.explanation: Correct in the ideal differential model. Twisting and cable balance help common-mode rejection; real receivers reject interference only to the extent their balance and performance allow.

options.text: Common four-pair building-cabling Ethernet standards support 100 m channels with the required category and installation quality
options.explanation: Correct for those specified PHYs/channels, not every Ethernet variant or transceiver.

options.text: Every copper cable propagates signals faster than every optical fibre, guaranteeing lower end-to-end latency
options.explanation: False. Velocity depends on construction and optical wavelength; some copper cables are faster than ordinary glass and others slower. PHY processing also contributes to latency.

options.text: The signal travels at the speed the electrons move through the wire
options.explanation: The signal is a guided electromagnetic wave; drift velocity is a different quantity depending on the current and conductor.

questions.workedExample: The receiver compares the two wires. Interference added equally to both does not change their difference in the ideal model; real rejection depends on balance and receiver performance. Check the particular Ethernet PHY and cable specification for reach. Signal speed is an electromagnetic propagation property, rather than electron drift speed; complete latency also includes electronics.

questions.prompt: You carry a laptop from next to a Wi-Fi access point to a room 25 m away through two walls. Throughput falls from 600 Mbit/s to 60 Mbit/s. Which are plausible contributing mechanisms, requiring measurements to confirm? Select all that apply.

options.text: Received signal strength falls with distance and wall absorption, so SNR drops
options.explanation: Plausible. Distance, obstacles and multipath can reduce received signal and SNR; the exact indoor loss is not determined by a free-space formula alone.

options.text: With lower SNR, the radios switch to modulation with fewer bits per symbol (for example from 1024-QAM down to 16-QAM)
options.explanation: Plausible. Rate adaptation may choose a more robust modulation/coding scheme; it does not necessarily choose the densest constellation from SNR alone.

options.text: More frames are corrupted and must be retransmitted at the link layer
options.explanation: Plausible. More unsuccessful attempts can consume airtime. A retransmission can deliver previously lost data; goodput counts each useful byte once and includes the cost of failed attempts.

options.text: Propagation delay over 25 m slows each frame down
options.explanation: 25 m at nearly c is about 83 nanoseconds. That's negligible against frame times of tens to hundreds of microseconds; distance hurts through signal strength, not travel time.

questions.workedExample: Weaker signal, a lower selected PHY rate and extra retries are plausible mechanisms. The extra 25 m propagation is only about 83 ns and cannot explain the stated tenfold throughput drop. Measure signal/noise, PHY rate, retries, contention and backhaul before diagnosing or choosing a fix; a mesh node is not a guaranteed remedy.

lessons.title: Fibre reach, loss and pulse speed
lessons.summary: Compare fibre modes, interpret optical loss and explain how group index affects pulse speed.
lessons.body:
## Fibre

An optical fibre is a glass **core** surrounded by **cladding** of slightly lower refractive index. The refractive-index structure guides optical modes; **total internal reflection** is a useful ray-model explanation, particularly for multimode fibre. A laser or LED switches on and off (or modulates phase and amplitude) to encode symbols.

- **Multi-mode fibre** has a wide core (50 or 62.5 µm). Light takes many paths ("modes") of slightly different length, so pulses spread out (modal dispersion). It is cheap with 850 nm optics and good for a few hundred metres: 10GBASE-SR reaches about 300 m on OM3 and 400 m on OM4.
- **Single-mode fibre** supports one spatial mode over its specified wavelength range; it is not literally one geometrical ray. Core diameter and mode-field diameter are distinct properties. With 1310 or 1550 nm lasers it reaches tens of kilometres directly, and thousands with amplifiers.
- For a hypothetical fibre loss of **0.2 dB/km**, an 80 km span loses 16 dB before connectors/splices. Actual loss is product- and wavelength-dependent; amplifier spacing also depends on the optical power/noise budget, not a universal distance.
- **Wavelength-division multiplexing** (DWDM) sends dozens of wavelengths through one fibre, each its own channel. Total capacity depends on channel count, modulation, coding, equipment and reach; no universal capacity figure is implied.
- The optical signal is not subject to electromagnetic pickup like copper wiring, but fibre can still be tapped or physically damaged. Fibre is not a substitute for encryption. Both optical and copper links are used in data centres.

Fibre loss is quoted in decibels because losses along a route then simply add. The surviving power fraction changes multiplicatively.

The hypothetical 80 km span has 16 dB loss, leaving about 2.5% of its launched optical power before connector and splice losses. A fixed number of decibels represents a multiplicative power change, rather than a fixed percentage of the original launch power.

```formula reference
A = αd
P_out / P_in = 10^(−A / 10)
where
A: total distributed attenuation in decibels
α: loss per kilometre, in decibels per kilometre, for the specified fibre and wavelength
d: span length in kilometres
P_out: received optical power in watts after the modelled span loss
P_in: launched optical power in watts
In words: distributed loss adds in decibels as the span gets longer; each additional ten decibels leaves one tenth of the power that would otherwise remain.
```

### Why pulses travel slower in glass

For pulse propagation, use the fibre’s **effective group index**, not simply the bulk phase refractive index. Corning’s July 2025 SMF-28 Ultra data sheet lists a typical group index of 1.4682 at 1550 nm. Rounding to 1.47 means that the pulse speed is the vacuum speed of light divided by 1.47.

Pulses therefore travel at about 68% of the vacuum speed of light in this example, taking about 4.9 microseconds per kilometre. A higher group index means slower pulse propagation.

Wavelength and fibre construction matter.

On copper, the signal is an electromagnetic wave guided by the conductors and dielectric. Its speed is not the electron drift velocity. **Velocity factor** depends on cable construction: copper is not universally slower than glass. For example, Belden 2433 specifies a nominal 72% of c, above the roughly 68% used in the glass-fibre example. Compare complete link latency, including PHY electronics, when choosing a medium.

> [!note] Lower propagation delay
> Radio in air travels close to c. Hollow-core fibre can also reduce propagation delay because much of its optical field travels through an air-filled region. Microsoft has reported Azure deployment. Exact universal hollow-core velocity and trading-route latency figures are omitted because they require a specific fibre, wavelength, route and measurement source.

## Key takeaways
- Fibre reach depends on mode, optics, attenuation and the optical budget.
- Group index determines pulse delay; copper velocity is construction-dependent.

## Further reading
