questions.prompt: Why do pulses in typical solid-glass telecommunications fibre propagate at about two-thirds of the speed of light (c)?

options.text: Because light bounces from side to side, so it travels a longer zig-zag path
options.explanation: A geometrical zig-zag explanation is not sufficient, especially for a single spatial mode. Pulse velocity depends on the effective group index.

options.text: Its effective group index is about 1.47, so pulses travel at about the speed of light divided by 1.47
options.explanation: Correct. The group index incorporates the relevant propagation/dispersion behaviour; the speed of light divided by 1.47 is about 0.68 of the speed of light.

options.text: Because the optical amplifiers along the route add delay
options.explanation: Amplifiers (EDFAs) add a tiny amount of delay, but the two-thirds figure applies over any length of glass, including a short patch cable with no amplifier.

options.text: Because the electrons in the fibre move slowly
options.explanation: There are no conduction electrons carrying the signal in fibre; it's light. (And in copper, electron drift speed isn't the signal speed either.)

questions.workedExample: The effective group index describes pulse propagation in the specified fibre and wavelength. A value near 1.47 means pulses travel more slowly than light in vacuum, at about 68% of that speed. It applies even to a short unamplified fibre; it is not explained merely by equipment delay or a literal zig-zag path. Use a fibre- and wavelength-specific value for precision.

questions.prompt: For a direct standard 10 Gbit/s link over a 2 km cable route, compare Cat6a/10GBASE-T, OM4/10GBASE-SR and single-mode/10GBASE-LR, without intermediate repeaters. Which listed pairing has the specified reach, assuming a compliant optical loss budget?

options.text: Cat6a twisted pair
options.explanation: 10GBASE-T is limited to 100 m. 2 km is twenty times too far without repeaters.

options.text: Multi-mode fibre
options.explanation: 10GBASE-SR over compliant OM4 supports 400 m, below this 2 km requirement.

options.text: Single-mode fibre
options.explanation: Correct for the specified 10GBASE-LR equipment and compliant single-mode channel, rated up to 10 km. Connector/splice loss and compatibility still matter.

options.text: Coaxial cable
options.explanation: Coax works for cable TV broadband, but 10 Gbit/s Ethernet over 2 km of coax isn't a standard option, and attenuation at those frequencies would be severe.

questions.workedExample: For these specified pairings, Cat6a/10GBASE-T supports up to 100 m, OM4/10GBASE-SR up to 400 m, and single-mode/10GBASE-LR up to 10 km. Choose the last for the 2 km route after checking equipment compatibility and optical loss budget; fibre type alone does not specify reach.

questions.prompt: Two equal fibre spans have the same loss in decibels. The second follows the first with no amplifier between them. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Each span subtracts the same fixed percentage of the original launch power
options.explanation: Each equal dB loss acts on the power entering that span, rather than subtracting a fixed share of the original launch.

options.text: The losses cancel because both are measured in decibels
options.explanation: Successive passive losses accumulate; they do not cancel.

options.text: The decibel losses add, while the surviving power fractions multiply
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed dB loss is a multiplicative reduction of the power entering each span.

options.text: A low attenuation figure alone proves the complete optical link will work
options.explanation: Launch power, receiver sensitivity, connectors, splices, dispersion and equipment compatibility still matter.

questions.workedExample: Follow the remaining power: the first span leaves some fraction; the second leaves the same fraction of what entered it. Decibel accounting turns these successive multiplicative losses into addition. Then check the complete optical budget and equipment constraints rather than treating distributed attenuation alone as proof of reach.

questions.prompt: A microwave route is shorter than an alternative solid-glass fibre route, and radio propagates faster than pulses in that glass. Counting propagation only, why can microwave have lower delay?

options.text: Its higher advertised bit rate makes every signal travel faster
options.explanation: Bit rate controls transmission time, not propagation speed along the specified medium.

options.text: Only distance matters; the medium's signal speed cannot affect delay
options.explanation: Both route length and signal speed matter.

options.text: It combines a shorter path with a higher propagation speed
options.explanation: Correct. Both specified differences reduce signal travel time.

options.text: Lower propagation alone proves the full link has better availability and capacity
options.explanation: Weather, frequency, antennas, equipment and route engineering require separate assessment.

questions.workedExample: Compare the path each signal travels, then the speed along that path. Here both comparisons favour microwave for propagation. That establishes only the modelled travel-time advantage: equipment latency, retransmissions, capacity and weather availability remain separate questions.

lessons.title: Ethernet frames and packet rate
lessons.summary: Explain padding, frame boundaries and why small frames stress packet-processing capacity.
lessons.body:
The link layer moves frames across a link or bridged LAN. Ethernet is a widely used family of link technologies with a common MAC framing model. Its PHYs and optional encapsulations vary; this lesson starts with ordinary untagged Ethernet II frames.

## The Ethernet frame

The following is the basic untagged format. Tagged/envelope frames and specific PHY rules need additional accounting.

| Field | Bytes | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Preamble | 7 | Clock sync |
| Start frame delimiter | 1 | "Frame starts now" |
| Destination MAC | 6 | Who it's for |
| Source MAC | 6 | Who sent it |
| EtherType | 2 | What's inside |
| Payload | 46–1500 | IP packet etc. |
| FCS | 4 | CRC-32 check |

- The **preamble** is alternating 1s and 0s that lets the receiver lock onto the bit clock. The **SFD** ends in two 1s, signalling that the frame proper begins. Neither is counted in the frame size.
- **Destination first**: a switch can begin a destination lookup early, though VLAN classification and other policy may require more header information. This enables **cut-through** switching, where forwarding begins before the whole frame has arrived.
- **EtherType** values of 1536 (`0x0600`) or more identify the payload protocol. Values of 1500 or less are interpreted as a *length* instead, the IEEE 802.3 length/LLC interpretation. Values 1501–1535 are neither a valid length in that range nor an EtherType.
- The **payload** is at least 46 bytes; shorter payloads are padded. So the smallest frame (destination to FCS) is 6 + 6 + 2 + 46 + 4 = **64 bytes** and the largest basic untagged frame here is **1518 bytes**; that is not a universal maximum for every Ethernet encapsulation.
- The **FCS** is a CRC-32 over the destination address through payload and pad (including any tags), excluding preamble/SFD and the FCS itself. A receiver that finds a mismatch silently drops the frame. Ordinary full-duplex Ethernet MAC service does not acknowledge/retransmit a frame after an FCS failure; recovering from loss is left to higher layers (the error-control units).

Use a nominal **inter-frame gap** of 96 bit-times (12 byte-times) for the steady-rate calculations here. Some PHYs use alignment/deficit-idle rules; gap timing is not literal extra payload bytes. So each frame costs 20 extra bytes of wire time: 8 for preamble and SFD, and 12 for the gap.

> [!example] Packet rates
> A minimum frame occupies 64 + 20 = 84 bytes of wire time. At 1 Gbit/s that allows up to about **1.49 million Ethernet frames per second**; at full size it is about 81,000 Ethernet frames per second. Router and firewall vendors quote "packets per second" figures for exactly this reason: small packets are the hard case.

The most frames a link can carry each second is its bit rate divided by the bits each frame occupies on the wire, overhead included:

```formula reference
f_max = R / (b(F + H))
where
f_max: the maximum frame rate, in Ethernet frames per second
R: the link rate, in bits per second; 1 Gbit/s = 10⁹ bits per second
F: the frame size from destination address to FCS, in bytes; 64 for a minimum frame, 1518 for a full-size one
b: eight bits per byte, converting byte counts into bit counts
H: nominal wire overhead beyond the frame, expressed as 20 equivalent bytes of wire time for preamble, SFD and gap
In words: at a fixed link bit rate, smaller frames arrive more often, so processing capacity must be checked in frames per second as well as bits per second; count preamble and gap in the wire-time budget.
```

## Key takeaways
- An ordinary untagged frame spans 64–1518 bytes from destination MAC through FCS.
- Minimum frames require more packets per second at a fixed line rate.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: A short ARP message is followed by padding in an ordinary untagged Ethernet frame. Why is the padding present?

options.text: ARP requires every address to be extended until the frame is full size
options.explanation: ARP's address fields have their own layout; padding belongs to the Ethernet framing boundary.

options.text: Ethernet requires a minimum frame size even when its payload protocol is short
options.explanation: Correct. The short message is padded to meet the minimum; this does not turn the pad into ARP data.

options.text: Preamble and start delimiter must appear inside the ARP payload
options.explanation: Preamble/start delimiter precede the Ethernet frame proper.

options.text: All Ethernet frames must be the maximum frame size
options.explanation: Ordinary basic untagged frames are variable-length within their permitted range.

questions.workedExample: Separate the payload message from the enclosing frame. ARP needs only its own fields, but Ethernet retains a minimum frame length. Padding fills the shortfall before the FCS, and the receiver uses the payload protocol's format or length to distinguish meaningful data. Captures may omit padding or FCS.

questions.prompt: A firewall reaches its advertised bit rate with large Ethernet frames. Why should you also test it with minimum-size frames at the same link bit rate?

options.text: Small frames arrive more often, increasing per-frame processing demand
options.explanation: Correct. At a fixed line rate, shorter frames mean more forwarding decisions and associated per-packet work each second.

options.text: Small frames remove all Ethernet overhead
options.explanation: Preamble, gap, headers and FCS still consume time, and overhead takes a larger share of a short frame.

options.text: Large-frame throughput proves every packet workload will have the same performance
options.explanation: Per-packet work, enabled features and traffic patterns can create different limits.

options.text: One packet's processing latency alone always determines aggregate throughput
options.explanation: Pipelining and parallel processing can decouple individual latency from aggregate packet rate.

questions.workedExample: Compare the work done once per byte with the work done once per frame. Short frames consume fewer wire-time units each, so a busy port presents frames more frequently. Check both bits per second and packets per second with the intended features and workload; one large-frame result does not establish every case.

lessons.title: Read MAC address bits
lessons.summary: Interpret individual/group and universal/local bits without treating an address as secure identity.
lessons.body:
## MAC addresses

A **MAC address** is 48 bits, written as six hex bytes, e.g. `3c:22:fb:11:22:33`.

- For an IEEE MA-L allocation, the first three bytes are an **OUI** assigned to an organisation, which assigns the remaining bits. Other allocation sizes and locally administered addresses do not follow a universal three-byte manufacturer rule.
- The least significant bit of the first byte is the **I/G bit**: 0 for an individual (unicast) address, 1 for a group (multicast) address.
- The next bit is the **U/L bit**: 0 for universally administered addressing (intended to be unique under its allocation rules, not proof of authenticity), 1 for a **locally administered** one.
- **Broadcast** is all ones: `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`. It addresses all stations in the broadcast domain, subject to filtering and policy.

```
first byte 0x3c = 0011 1100
                         ^^
             U/L = 0 ----+|
             I/G = 0 -----+
-> universal, unicast
```

Many phones and laptops support **private/randomised MAC addresses** for Wi-Fi; persistence, rotation and defaults depend on OS version and configuration. For locally administered **unicast** addresses, U/L is 1 and I/G is 0, so the second hex digit is 2, 6, A or E (for example `da:a1:19:...`). This reduces some cross-network tracking and can conflict with hardware-address allow-lists; it neither prevents all tracking nor makes a MAC a secure identity.

MAC addresses use **flat addressing**: they say nothing about where a device is. That is fine within a LAN but would not scale to the internet, which is why IP prefixes (hierarchically aggregated for routing, rather than a reliable geographical location) exist at layer 3.

## Key takeaways
- The lowest first-octet bit marks individual versus group addresses.
- Randomisation and local administration can conflict with allow-lists; MAC addresses are not authentication.

## Further reading

- [Network switch — Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_switch)

- [IEEE address-allocation guidelines](https://standards-support.ieee.org/hc/en-us/articles/4888705676564-Guidelines-for-Use-of-Extended-Unique-Identifier-EUI-Organizationally-Unique-Identifier-OUI-and-Company-ID-CID)
- [Cisco auto-negotiation and duplex guidance](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/lan-switching/ethernet/10561-3.html)
- [Cisco unicast flooding behaviour](https://www.cisco.com/c/en/us/support/docs/switches/catalyst-6000-series-switches/23563-143.html)
- [Apple private Wi-Fi address modes](https://support.apple.com/en-ie/102509)

questions.prompt: Which of these destination MAC addresses is a **multicast** (group) address?

options.explanation: 0x3c is 0011 1100. The least significant bit (I/G) is 0, so this is unicast.
0xda has the local-administration bit set and the group bit clear. It is locally administered unicast; that does not alone prove it was randomised.
0x00 has every bit clear, so this is a universally administered unicast address.
Correct: the I/G bit is 1. IPv4 mDNS address 224.0.0.251 maps here, but IPv4 multicast-to-MAC mapping is not one-to-one, so the MAC alone does not prove mDNS.

questions.workedExample:
Look only at the first byte, and at its lowest bit.

```
3c  0011 1100  I/G 0: unicast
da  1101 1010  I/G 0: unicast
00  0000 0000  I/G 0: unicast
01  0000 0001  I/G 1: multicast
```

A quick rule: if the **second hex digit is odd**, the address is multicast. Broadcast (`ff:ff:...`) is the special case of a group address with every bit set.

questions.prompt: Your office Wi-Fi only admits devices on a MAC allow-list. A user's new phone keeps getting refused, and the Wi-Fi management console shows it connecting from `da:a1:19:40:0b:7e`, which isn't the address printed in the phone's settings. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: The phone is faulty and corrupting its MAC address
options.explanation: A consistent locally administered address is compatible with deliberate configuration or privacy behaviour. The bit pattern alone cannot prove or rule out all faults.

options.text: Someone is spoofing the phone's address
options.explanation: Spoofing is possible, but not established by these observations. Check the phone’s current private-address setting before assuming an attacker.

options.text: The phone is using a randomised, locally administered MAC for this network
options.explanation: This is a plausible likely cause on a privacy-enabled phone. The local bit identifies administration type, not proof of randomisation.

options.text: The address is a multicast address used during Wi-Fi association
options.explanation: Check the I/G bit: 0xda ends in 0, so this is unicast. Multicast addresses have an odd second hex digit.

questions.workedExample: 0xda ends in binary 10: individual/unicast and locally administered. Check the device’s per-network private-address setting and any fixed/rotating mode. Resolve enrolment using the network’s supported device-authentication policy. A MAC can be changed or copied, so an allow-list alone is not strong authentication.

lessons.title: Collisions, backoff and full duplex
lessons.summary: Explain legacy CSMA/CD timing and why full-duplex links use different rules.
lessons.body:
## CSMA/CD: how shared Ethernet worked

Original Ethernet put every host on one shared coaxial cable (later, one hub). Only one host could transmit at once, so they needed a rule for taking turns: **carrier-sense multiple access with collision detection**.

1. **Carrier sense**: listen; if someone is transmitting, wait.
2. When the line is idle, transmit.
3. **Collision detect**: while transmitting, listen. If the signal on the wire doesn't match what you're sending, another host started at nearly the same moment. Stop and send a 32-bit **jam signal** so everyone notices.
4. **Binary exponential backoff**: after each collision, wait a random whole number of **slot times** before retrying, still obeying carrier-sense rules. The range of possible waits doubles with every collision on this frame, up to a cap. At 10/100 Mbit/s the slot is 512 bit-times; historical half-duplex Gigabit uses 4096 bit-times. Give up after 16 attempts.

```formula reference
K ∈ {0, 1, …, 2^{min(n, 10)} − 1}
t_wait = K t_slot
where
K: the number of slot times to wait, chosen at random (each value equally likely)
∈: "is one of": K is picked from the set in braces
…: and every whole number in between
n: how many collisions this frame has suffered so far (1 after the first)
min: the minimum, the smaller of the two values; it stops the range growing after the 10th collision
t_wait: the backoff wait before trying again, in seconds
t_slot: the duration of one slot, in seconds: 512 bit-times, or 51.2 µs (microseconds), at 10 Mbit/s
In words: after the first collision wait 0 or 1 slots, after the second 0–3, after the third 0–7, and so on, doubling up to 0–1023 slots from the 10th collision onwards.
```

Backoff adapts to load: with two hosts colliding, after the first collision each picks 0 or 1, so they avoid each other half the time. Repeated collisions widen the range quickly.

### Why the minimum frame is 64 bytes

A sender only knows about a collision if it is still transmitting when the colliding signal gets back to it. The worst case is a collision at the far end of the network: the signal must travel there and back. So the transmission time of the shortest frame must be at least the maximum round-trip time:

```formula reference
L_min / R ≥ (2d_max) / v
where
L_min: the minimum frame length, in bits; 64 bytes = 512 bits
R: the link rate, in bits per second; 10 Mbit/s = 10⁷ bits per second
d_max: the largest distance between two hosts on the shared segment, in metres
v: the signal speed in the cable, in metres per second (about 2 × 10⁸ m/s)
≥: greater than or equal to
In words: sending the smallest frame must take at least as long as a signal needs to reach the far end and come back, so faster links need shorter networks or longer minimum frames.
```

At 10 Mbit/s, 64 bytes (512 bits) takes 51.2 µs to send. The **slot time**, propagation and repeater delays together constrain the collision domain; physical topology rules cannot be inferred from cable speed alone. At gigabit speeds, 512 bits takes only 0.512 µs (the link is a hundred times faster than 10 Mbit/s, so a frame takes a hundredth of the time), which would limit a shared segment to a few tens of metres; half-duplex gigabit worked around this with "carrier extension", an historical half-duplex mechanism distinct from modern full-duplex operation.

### Why it no longer matters

A common modern Ethernet arrangement is a **full-duplex** point-to-point link between a host and a switch port. Other Ethernet deployments include switch links and shared-medium PHYs. Each endpoint can send and receive concurrently. Some PHYs separate directions physically; 1000BASE-T uses both directions on the same four pairs with echo cancellation. A shared half-duplex collision domain is absent. CSMA/CD is switched off. 10 Gigabit Ethernet and faster do not support half duplex at all.

> [!warning] Duplex mismatch
> On legacy 10/100BASE-T links, if one end is forced to full duplex and the auto-negotiating peer detects speed but falls back to half duplex, the half-duplex side sees "collisions" whenever both send. The half-duplex side can back off and report late collisions; the full-duplex side may report FCS or alignment errors. Bidirectional throughput can suffer even when small pings succeed; exact counters and symptoms depend on timing and implementation. Use compatible settings, normally auto-negotiation at both ends. Do not generalise the legacy fallback behaviour to every Gigabit PHY; follow the equipment requirements.

## Key takeaways
- Legacy collision detection needs enough transmission time for a round-trip collision signal.
- Full-duplex Ethernet has no shared half-duplex collision domain or CSMA/CD backoff.

lessons.title: Learn, forward, filter or flood
lessons.summary: Trace a simple learning switch and explain its omitted policies and attack limitations.
lessons.body:
## Switches and MAC learning

A **switch** connects many links and forwards frames between them. Unlike a hub, which repeated every bit out of every port, a bridge can restrict known unicast forwarding, while some traffic is still flooded. To do that it builds a **MAC address table** (often called the CAM table) by watching traffic:

Assume valid frames, one VLAN, eligible forwarding ports, ordinary learning and no configured exceptions.

1. **Learn**: when a frame arrives on port P with source MAC S, record "S is reachable via P".
2. **Forward**: look up the destination MAC.
   - Known, on another port: send it out of that port only.
   - Known, on the same port it arrived on: drop it (filter).
   - Unknown, broadcast or (by default) multicast: use **Ethernet flooding** to copy it to eligible forwarding ports in the same VLAN, excluding ingress. Multicast snooping/filtering can narrow the set.
3. **Age**: remove dynamic entries after the configured ageing interval when they are not refreshed. Static entries and topology-change handling have different rules.

Basic learning can work automatically, but VLANs, spanning tree, security and management still require suitable configuration.

This toy models ordinary unicast labels plus an unknown broadcast label on one VLAN. It omits FCS validation, MAC-format checks, multicast policy, aging, VLANs, spanning tree, capacity and special ingress-reflection modes.

```python
class Switch:
    def __init__(self, ports):
        self.ports = tuple(ports)
        self.table = {}  # mac -> port

    def receive(self, port, src, dst):
        if port not in self.ports:
            raise ValueError("unknown port")
        # Source traffic refreshes its
        # location.
        self.table[src] = port  # learn
        # Destination lookup chooses the
        # output.
        if dst in self.table:
            out = self.table[dst]
            if out == port:
                return []  # filter
            return [out]
        # unknown or broadcast: flood
        return [p for p in self.ports
                if p != port]


# Unknown B floods; its reply teaches port
# 2.
sw = Switch([1, 2, 3, 4])
print(sw.receive(1, "A", "B"))  # [2, 3, 4]
print(sw.receive(2, "B", "A"))  # [1]
print(sw.receive(1, "A", "B"))  # [2]
```

The first frame floods because B is unknown. B's reply teaches the switch where B is, and from then on traffic between A and B goes only between ports 1 and 2.

Hardware forwarding capacity and latency depend on the switch and enabled features. **Store-and-forward** receives and checks the full frame before forwarding. **Cut-through** can begin earlier and may propagate part or all of a frame later found corrupt; its latency is not universally below one microsecond.

> [!warning] MAC-table exhaustion
> Large numbers of spoofed source addresses can exhaust learning capacity. Depending on the device and configuration, unknown unicast may then be flooded within its VLAN, exposing frames to additional ports or causing disruption. Existing learned entries need not all disappear, and flooding is not guaranteed. Configured per-port learning limits and appropriate violation actions can constrain this attack; encrypted payloads remain protected when the encryption is correctly implemented and endpoints are uncompromised.

## Key takeaways
- Learning uses the source; destination lookup determines forwarding.
- Unknown traffic flooding, ageing and exhaustion behaviour depend on policy and implementation.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: A switch has just been powered on, so its MAC table is empty. A frame arrives on port 3 addressed to a MAC it has never seen. What does the switch do? Assume a valid unknown-unicast frame, ordinary learning, one VLAN, all listed ports forwarding, and no isolation, filtering or hairpin mode.

options.text: Drops the frame, because the destination is unknown
options.explanation: That's what a router does with an unroutable packet. A switch floods unknown destinations so that the frame still arrives; the reply then teaches it where the host is.

options.text: Sends an ARP request to find out which port the destination is on
options.explanation: Basic destination bridging learns from source MACs; it does not use ARP to resolve an output port. A switch acting as an IP endpoint/router can separately use ARP.

options.text: Records the source MAC against port 3, then floods the frame out of every port except port 3
options.explanation: Correct. Learning happens on every frame from its source address, and an unknown destination is flooded everywhere except back where it came from.

options.text: Floods the frame out of every port including port 3
options.explanation: In the stipulated ordinary bridging mode, the ingress port is excluded. Special hairpin/reflection modes are outside this question.

questions.workedExample:
1. **Learn**: the source MAC is now known to be reachable via port 3.
2. **Look up** the destination: not in the table.
3. **Flood**: copy the frame to every other port.

When the destination replies, its source MAC is learned on its port, and from then on frames to it go out of that one port only. Learning can be automatic, but suitable VLAN, spanning-tree and security configuration is still required.

questions.prompt:
A 4-port switch starts with an empty MAC table. Host A is on port 1, B on port 2 and C on port 3. These frames are sent in order:

```
1. A -> B
2. B -> A
3. C -> ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
4. A -> C
```

Out of which port(s) does frame 4 leave? Use the lesson’s toy switch and assume no aging or filtering between frames.

options.text: Ports 2, 3 and 4 (flooded)
options.explanation: C has never been a destination, but it has been a *source*: frame 3 taught the switch that C is on port 3. Switches learn from source addresses.

options.text: Port 3 only
options.explanation: Correct. After frame 3, the table holds A→1, B→2 and C→3, so frame 4 is forwarded to port 3 alone.

options.text: Ports 2 and 3
options.explanation: There is no reason to send it to B's port. If the switch didn't know C it would flood to 2, 3 and 4; since it does, it sends only to 3.

options.text: None: it is dropped because C sent a broadcast
options.explanation: A broadcast doesn't stop a host from receiving unicast. The broadcast was flooded, and its source address was learned like any other.

questions.workedExample:
Trace the table after each frame:

```
# frame      table          out
1 A->B     A:1            2,3,4
2 B->A     A:1 B:2        1
3 C->bcast A:1 B:2 C:3    1,2,4
4 A->C     (same)         3
```

Frame 3 is a broadcast, so it floods regardless, but its source still teaches the switch that C is on port 3. Frame 4 therefore goes to **port 3 only**.

questions.prompt: An attacker on one access port runs a tool that sends hundreds of thousands of Ethernet frames per second, each from a different random source MAC. Which of these are true? Select all that apply. Consider possible behaviour of an ordinarily flooding switch without existing per-port learning limits, rather than a guarantee for every device.

options.text: Table exhaustion can prevent new learning or cause eviction, potentially increasing unknown-unicast flooding
options.explanation: True as a possible effect. Existing learned destinations may still be forwarded normally; capacity and overflow policies vary.

options.text: If affected unknown-unicast frames are flooded to the attacker’s eligible VLAN port, the attacker can capture those frames
options.explanation: True under that condition. The attack does not automatically expose all unicast traffic or bypass VLAN forwarding policy.

options.text: Enforced per-port MAC limits with suitable violation actions can constrain source-address flooding from that port
options.explanation: True. The protection depends on configuration and implementation; it is not a guarantee against every disruption or attack.

options.text: The attacker can also read traffic in other VLANs on the same switch
options.explanation: Flooding stays within the VLAN. The MAC table is typically per-VLAN in effect, and frames are never flooded to ports in other VLANs.

options.text: The attack also lets the attacker read the contents of TLS connections
options.explanation: Frame capture alone does not decrypt properly secured TLS application data; exposed metadata and endpoint compromise are separate issues.

questions.workedExample: Spoofed sources can consume learning capacity. If legitimate destinations then lack table entries and the switch floods unknown unicast, eligible ports in that VLAN may receive those frames. Existing entries, capacity rules and suppression settings affect the result. Per-port learning limits can contain the source flood. Capturing frames does not itself decrypt properly secured TLS payloads.

lessons.title: VLAN tags and path MTU
lessons.summary: Separate VLAN broadcast domains and diagnose size-dependent failures after encapsulation.
lessons.body:
## VLANs

A basic single-VLAN bridge joins eligible ports into one broadcast domain; port isolation and filtering can further restrict connectivity. A **VLAN** (virtual LAN) splits one physical switch, or a set of switches, into several isolated LANs. Typical uses: separate staff, guest Wi-Fi, phones and servers without separate hardware.

IEEE **802.1Q** inserts a 4-byte **VLAN tag** after the source MAC:

| Field | Bits | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| TPID | 16 | `0x8100`: "tagged" |
| PCP | 3 | Priority (QoS) |
| DEI | 1 | Drop eligible |
| VID | 12 | VLAN ID |

- The 12-bit VID allows 4096 values; 0 indicates priority tagging without a VLAN identifier and 4095 is reserved, leaving **4094 assignable VLAN IDs**. Equipment may support fewer active VLANs.
- Adding one tag to a maximum-size basic 1518-byte frame produces 1522 bytes; additional encapsulation has its own limits.
- An ordinary **access port** presents one untagged data VLAN to a host; voice VLANs, priority tags and vendor-specific configurations are exceptions.
- A **trunk port** carries many VLANs between switches (or to a router or hypervisor), usually with tags distinguishing VLANs. Depending on configuration, untagged traffic may use a native VLAN or be rejected; a native VLAN can also be tagged.
- Hosts in different VLANs cannot talk at layer 2 at all. Traffic between them must go through a **router** (or a layer 3 switch), where it can be filtered.

Large providers outgrew 4094. **802.1ad** ("QinQ") stacks a second tag (TPID `0x88A8`), and data centres use **VXLAN**, which carries Ethernet frames inside UDP with a 24-bit segment ID, allowing about 16 million.

## MTU

The **MTU** (maximum transmission unit) is the largest payload a link can carry in one frame. For standard Ethernet it is **1500 bytes**: the IP packet, not counting Ethernet's own 18 bytes of header and FCS.

- **Jumbo frames** raise the MTU, typically to about 9000 bytes. Fewer, larger frames can reduce per-packet work (interrupt moderation and offloads mean interrupts are not necessarily one per frame), and slightly less header overhead, so storage networks and data-centre fabrics often use them. They are not part of the IEEE standard, and every traversed link/interface must support the sizes actually sent, or the sender must adapt to a smaller path MTU; configured MTUs need not all be identical.
- An **MTU mismatch** can produce a black-hole failure if fragmentation or path-MTU adaptation does not resolve it: small packets (pings, TCP handshakes, short requests) work, but full-size packets are dropped. Connections open and then hang as soon as real data flows. Tunnels (VPNs, VXLAN) cause the same thing by quietly shrinking the effective MTU.

The IP module covers how hosts discover the path MTU and what happens when that discovery fails.

## Key takeaways
- VLAN tags distinguish logical link-layer domains; routing connects them.
- Tunnels add overhead, so unresolved path-MTU constraints can break large packets.

questions.prompt: Which statements about IEEE 802.1Q VLAN tagging are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: A single tag adds four bytes: a 1518-byte basic frame becomes 1522 bytes
options.explanation: Correct. TPID (2 bytes) plus PCP, DEI and VID (2 bytes) are inserted after the source MAC.

options.text: The VLAN ID is 16 bits, allowing 65,536 VLANs
options.explanation: The VID is 12 bits. The other 4 bits of the tag control field are PCP (3) and DEI (1).

options.text: Hosts on access ports normally send and receive untagged frames
options.explanation: Correct for ordinary untagged access-port data service. Internal classification and egress tagging depend on port configuration; voice VLANs and priority tags are exceptions.

options.text: Two hosts in different VLANs on the same switch can reach each other if their IP addresses are in the same subnet
options.explanation: VLANs separate layer 2 completely: no frames, not even broadcasts or ARP, cross between them. Matching IP subnets don't help; traffic must be routed between VLANs.

options.text: There are 4094 usable VLAN IDs
options.explanation: Correct as the assignable ID space: 1–4094. VID 0 carries priority without a VLAN ID; 4095 is reserved. Hardware may support fewer simultaneous VLANs.

questions.workedExample:
The tag layout:

```
TPID 0x8100 | PCP 3 | DEI 1 | VID 12
  16 bits   |  -------16 bits------ 
```

- 4 bytes in total: 1518 + 4 = 1522.
- VID: 2¹² = 4096, minus priority-only VID 0 and reserved 4095 = 4094.
- Ordinary access ports carry untagged data; trunk/native/voice-tag behaviour depends on configuration.
- Between VLANs you need a router or layer 3 switch, which is precisely what makes VLANs useful for isolation.

questions.prompt: After you move a service behind a new site-to-site VPN, users report that the login page loads and small API calls work, but downloading reports hangs forever. `ping` to the server works. Which hypothesis most directly explains this size-dependent pattern and should be tested?

options.text: The server's CPU is overloaded by report generation
options.explanation: Server work is another possible cause of hangs, but the new tunnel and size-dependent pattern make path MTU a strong hypothesis to test, not a diagnosis by elimination.

options.text: An MTU problem: the tunnel's overhead means full-size 1500-byte packets no longer fit and are being dropped
options.explanation: This is a strong hypothesis: tunnel overhead can create a path-MTU failure when fragmentation or PMTU adaptation does not resolve it. Confirm with size-dependent tests and captures.

options.text: The VPN is blocking TCP, so only ICMP gets through
options.explanation: Working web/API traffic rules out a blanket claim that only ICMP passes. Confirm the actual transport: web traffic can use TCP or QUIC over UDP.

options.text: A duplex mismatch on the VPN appliance
options.explanation: A duplex problem is possible on some links, but these observations alone do not establish it. Check counters and packet sizes rather than ruling it out categorically.

questions.workedExample: A tunnel adds overhead. If the resulting packet exceeds an underlay MTU and neither fragmentation nor path-MTU adaptation succeeds, small exchanges may pass while large ones stall. On Linux, an authorised IPv4 test can use `ping -4 -s 1472 -M do <destination>`: 1472 payload + 8 ICMP + 20 IPv4 = 1500 bytes, without IP options. Failure alone is not proof of MTU trouble because ICMP can be filtered. Confirm with size variation, captures and tunnel settings; fix MTU/PMTU handling, or use TCP MSS adjustment where appropriate (it does not fix all UDP traffic).

lessons.title: Resolve the IPv4 next hop
lessons.summary: Choose the next-hop MAC and build the 28-byte Ethernet/IPv4 ARP message.
lessons.body:
The VLAN and MTU lesson separated link delivery from IP routing. A host now wants to send an IP packet to `192.168.1.1`, but an Ethernet frame needs a destination **MAC** address. Something has to translate one into the other. On IPv4 that is the **Address Resolution Protocol** (ARP, RFC 826, from 1982).

This unit chooses the next hop and constructs the ARP message. Later units cover cache state, spoofing defences and the switching loops that spanning tree prevents.

## Which MAC do I need?

Before sending, a host selects a route. In the simple case with only a connected subnet route and a default route:

- **Same subnet**: it needs the destination host's own MAC.
- **Different subnet**: it needs the MAC of its **default gateway** (router). The IP header still says the final destination; only the frame is addressed to the router.

```
laptop 192.168.1.20/24 -> 93.184.215.14

frame:  dst = router's MAC
packet: dst = 93.184.215.14
```

A prefix length says how many leading address bits identify the network. In the simple IPv4 examples, /24 corresponds to mask `255.255.255.0`, while /16 corresponds to `255.255.0.0`. A mistakenly broad connected prefix can make a host try direct ARP for a destination that actually needs a router. Without proxy ARP or another applicable route, nobody on its VLAN answers for that remote address.

On routed Ethernet hops the link-layer addresses identify the local next hop. Ordinary IP forwarding preserves source and destination IP addresses; NAT changes them, and tunnels add an outer packet. Other link technologies need not use Ethernet MAC addresses.

## How ARP works

1. The host looks in its **ARP cache** (`ip neigh` on Linux, `arp -a` on macOS and Windows).
2. On a miss, it broadcasts an **ARP request** to `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`: "Who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.20."
3. Hosts in the broadcast domain can receive it, subject to filtering and isolation. Normally the owner of 192.168.1.1 sends a **unicast ARP reply**: "192.168.1.1 is at `a4:91:b1:...`."
4. The asker caches the answer. RFC 826 updates an existing sender mapping before testing the opcode, and adds a new mapping when the receiver is the target. Implementations can impose additional checks; not every receiving host learns from every request.

The packet travels directly in an Ethernet frame with EtherType `0x0806`. It is not an IP packet. For IPv4 over Ethernet it is 28 bytes:

```python
import ipaddress
import struct

def arp_request(src_mac, src_ip, dst_ip):
    if len(src_mac) != 6:
        raise ValueError("need 6 MAC bytes")
    # Pack fields without Ethernet framing.
    return struct.pack(
        "!HHBBH6s4s6s4s",
        1,          # HTYPE: Ethernet
        0x0800,     # PTYPE: IPv4
        6, 4,       # HLEN, PLEN
        1,          # OPER: 1 = request
        src_mac,
        ipaddress.IPv4Address(
            src_ip).packed,
        bytes(6),   # target MAC: unknown
        ipaddress.IPv4Address(
            dst_ip).packed)

pkt = arp_request(
    bytes.fromhex("3c22fb112233"),
    "192.168.1.20", "192.168.1.1")
print(len(pkt))  # 28

# Group the raw message for visual
# inspection.
for i in range(0, 28, 12):
    print(pkt[i:i + 12].hex(" ", 4))
# 00010800 06040001 3c22fb11
# 2233c0a8 01140000 00000000
# c0a80101
```

`c0a80114` is 192.168.1.20 and `c0a80101` is 192.168.1.1. A reply has the same layout with the OPER (operation) field set to 2 and the target MAC filled in. On basic untagged Ethernet, a 28-byte ARP message needs 18 bytes of padding to form a 64-byte frame including the header and FCS. VLAN tags change the framing calculation; captures may omit padding or FCS.

## Key takeaways
- Routing chooses the next hop before ARP resolves its IPv4 address on Ethernet.
- An initial request is normally broadcast and the owner’s normal reply unicast.

questions.prompt: A laptop is `192.168.1.20/24` with default gateway `192.168.1.1`. It wants to send a packet to `8.8.8.8` and its ARP cache is empty. Which IP address does it put in its ARP request? Assume ordinary unicast Ethernet, only connected and default routes, and no proxy ARP.

options.explanation: The selected next hop is the default gateway. The laptop resolves that address, not the remote destination.
Correct. The destination is off-subnet, so the frame goes to the default gateway. The laptop ARPs for the gateway's MAC; the IP header still says 8.8.8.8.
That is the subnet's broadcast IP. ARP requests go to the broadcast *MAC* `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`, but they ask about a specific IP.

options.text: None: it asks DNS for the MAC address
options.explanation: Ordinary DNS name resolution does not resolve the Ethernet next-hop mapping; ARP does.

questions.workedExample:
1. Apply the mask: 192.168.1.20/24 is in 192.168.1.0/24.
2. Is 8.8.8.8 in 192.168.1.0/24? No.
3. So the next hop is the gateway, 192.168.1.1, and the laptop needs **its** MAC.
4. ARP request: "Who has 192.168.1.1? Tell 192.168.1.20."

The resulting frame has the router's MAC as destination and 8.8.8.8 as the IP destination. The router will build a fresh frame for its next link.

questions.prompt: For an initial Ethernet/IPv4 ARP lookup with no cache entry, proxy ARP or address conflict, how are the request and normal reply addressed?

options.text: Both are broadcast to `ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff`
options.explanation: The initial lookup request is broadcast. The normal reply is unicast; other ARP uses can include broadcast replies or unicast validation requests.

options.text: The request is unicast to the router, which replies on the target's behalf
options.explanation: The asker doesn't know any MAC for the target yet, so it can't unicast. Routers don't answer ARP for other hosts unless proxy ARP is configured.

options.text: The request is broadcast; the reply is unicast to the requester
options.explanation: Correct. Eligible hosts can receive the broadcast, subject to filtering or isolation. Under the stated assumptions, the target replies directly to the sender’s MAC.

options.text: Both are sent inside IP packets to the subnet broadcast address
options.explanation: ARP isn't carried in IP at all. It sits directly in an Ethernet frame with EtherType 0x0806; it has to work before IP delivery on the LAN is possible.

questions.workedExample: The initial request uses the broadcast destination and contains the sender IP and MAC. The addressed host can reply directly to that MAC. Each ARP message is 28 bytes. On basic untagged Ethernet, header, padding and FCS make a minimum 64-byte frame; capture formats may omit padding or FCS.

questions.prompt: A server is mistakenly configured as `192.168.1.20` with mask `255.255.0.0` (/16), but the network is really `192.168.1.0/24`. It tries to reach `192.168.5.10`, which is on a different VLAN behind the router. The router has proxy ARP disabled. What happens? Assume no more-specific routes, no ARP spoofing, and a correct default gateway otherwise.

options.text: It works normally, because the router forwards all traffic between subnets
options.explanation: On this ordinary Ethernet next hop the host must address its Ethernet frames to the router. The mistaken connected route instead triggers direct ARP for the remote host.

options.text: The server ARPs for 192.168.1.1 and sends via the gateway
options.explanation: That's what would happen with the correct /24 mask. With /16 the server believes 192.168.5.10 is on its own subnet and skips the gateway.

options.text: The server broadcasts an ARP for 192.168.5.10, nobody on its VLAN answers, and the connection fails
options.explanation: Correct. With /16, 192.168.5.10 looks local, so the server ARPs for it directly. The real host is on another VLAN, beyond the broadcast domain, so no reply comes.

options.text: The switch forwards the ARP to the other VLAN, and the target replies
options.explanation: Normal VLAN bridging does not carry this broadcast into the other VLAN; no proxy is configured to answer here.

questions.workedExample:
1. Server's view: 192.168.1.20/16 → its subnet is 192.168.0.0 to 192.168.255.255.
2. Is 192.168.5.10 in that? Yes, so the server treats it as local.
3. It broadcasts "Who has 192.168.5.10?" in its own VLAN.
4. The target is in another VLAN, so it never sees the request. No reply, so no frame can be sent and the connection times out.
5. Meanwhile, hosts in 192.168.1.x still work, which is what makes wrong masks confusing to debug.

A suitably configured proxy ARP router could answer for the remote host and mask the error, provided forwarding and return routing also work.

lessons.title: ARP cache state and announcements
lessons.summary: Distinguish stale reachability state, address probes and failover announcements.
lessons.body:
### The cache

Cache lifetime and reachability are separate. Linux's default 30-second base reachable time is randomised to 15–45 seconds. Becoming **stale** does not immediately delete an entry or require resolution before the next packet: Linux can send using it, then seek confirmation. Other systems and configurations differ. A stale mapping can disrupt delivery until it is updated or resolved again.

### Gratuitous ARP

An unsolicited ARP announcement advertises a host’s own address; it is commonly called **gratuitous ARP**. Address-conflict detection also uses a distinct probe before claiming an address. RFC 5227 specifies both:

- **ARP probe**: before using an address, send a request for it with sender IP 0.0.0.0. A conflicting request or reply, or another host probing the same target address, can reveal a conflict. It is not enough to check replies alone.
- **ARP announcement**: broadcast an ARP request with both sender and target IP set to the announced address, allowing receiving hosts to refresh applicable mappings.

Announcements can help move a virtual IP during failover. With different physical MAC addresses, neighbours need the new mapping. VRRP uses a shared virtual MAC; then switch forwarding tables must learn its new location. Failure detection, filtering and implementation affect recovery time.

> [!note] Content omitted after review
> A universal millisecond failover time and cross-product ARP-cache defaults are omitted because they depend on versions, configuration and measurements not established here.

## Key takeaways
- Stale does not mean an entry is immediately deleted or unusable.
- Probes detect conflicts; announcements refresh mappings, while a shared virtual MAC also needs switch relearning.

questions.prompt: Two load balancers share a VIP using their distinct physical MACs, without a shared virtual MAC. After failover, local clients can establish new connections, but external clients cannot. A capture shows the upstream router still sending VIP traffic to the failed node's MAC. Which explanation fits?

options.text: DNS still points at the old load balancer's IP
options.explanation: The VIP itself hasn't changed; only which machine owns it. DNS maps names to IPs and is unaffected by which MAC answers for that IP.

options.text: The router's ARP cache still maps the VIP to the failed machine's MAC, because it ignored or never received the gratuitous ARP
options.explanation: Correct. The capture establishes a stale IP-to-MAC mapping. An announcement may have been lost, filtered or rejected. How long it persists depends on neighbour handling and configuration.

options.text: The router needs a new route to the VIP
options.explanation: The VIP is on the same subnet as before, so the router's route is unchanged. What's wrong is the link-layer delivery on the final hop.

options.text: TCP connections can't survive failover, so clients must reconnect
options.explanation: Existing connection survival depends on replicated state. Failure of new connections plus frames addressed to the old MAC identifies a link-layer delivery problem.

questions.workedExample: The VIP is unchanged, but its active physical MAC has changed. Local clients learned the new mapping; the capture shows the router has not. Check announcement delivery, neighbour-update policy and any static mapping. A shared virtual MAC avoids changing this ARP mapping, but then switches must learn the virtual MAC's new port. Neither design guarantees an immediate recovery time.

lessons.title: ARP spoofing and layered defences
lessons.summary: Assess poisoning evidence and distinguish inspection, isolation and authenticated encryption.
lessons.body:
## ARP spoofing

ARP has no authentication at all. A host with access to the link can claim a false mapping. Without defensive checks, receivers may update existing entries from unsolicited messages. That is what makes gratuitous ARP failover work, and it is also the attack.

**ARP spoofing** (or ARP cache poisoning) goes like this:

1. The attacker, on the same LAN, sends the victim repeated replies: "192.168.1.1 is at *attacker's MAC*".
2. It sends the router: "192.168.1.20 is at *attacker's MAC*".
3. Both now send their frames to the attacker, which forwards them on so nothing appears broken.

```
before:  victim ---------> router
after:   victim -> ATTACKER -> router
```

The attacker is now a **man in the middle**. It can read unencrypted traffic, modify it, or drop it (a denial of service). Properly authenticated TLS protects application contents, but does not hide all metadata or prevent the intermediary from dropping traffic. The attack alone does not defeat TLS authentication.

> [!warning] Why this matters on shared networks
> A shared layer 2 network can expose peers to forged ARP messages unless isolation or inspection blocks them. The network location alone does not establish that an attack is possible or occurring.

### Defences

| Defence | How it helps |
|---|---|
| Encryption (TLS, SSH, VPN) | Authenticated encryption protects contents and integrity, not availability or all metadata |
| Dynamic ARP Inspection | Configured switches validate ARP against trusted bindings or ARP ACLs |
| Static ARP entries | Can prevent dynamic replacement of that mapping; do not prevent MAC impersonation or other attacks |
| Client isolation, small VLANs | Fewer hosts can reach you at layer 2 |

**Dynamic ARP Inspection** (DAI) is one switch defence. With **DHCP snooping**, the switch watches DHCP and records which IP was leased to which MAC on which port. DAI checks ARP on configured untrusted ports against bindings; static-address hosts may require ARP ACLs. Trusted ports and incorrect bindings need care. Monitoring tools such as arpwatch alert when a mapping changes.

IPv6 uses **Neighbor Discovery**: initial address resolution uses ICMPv6 neighbour solicitations to a solicited-node multicast address; reachability probes can be unicast. Unauthenticated ND also has spoofing risks. ND inspection and SEND address aspects of this problem. RA Guard filters router advertisements; it is not a general defence against forged neighbour advertisements.

## Key takeaways
- ARP itself does not authenticate mappings; a duplicate MAC mapping alone is not proof of attack.
- DAI, isolation and authenticated encryption protect different aspects; RA Guard is not general ND inspection.

questions.prompt: A laptop sees both `192.168.1.1` (its gateway) and `192.168.1.66` mapped to `7e:31:9a:04:c2:10` in its ARP cache. No other evidence is available. What can you conclude?

options.text: The mapping is definitely normal
options.explanation: Multiple IPs can legitimately share a MAC, but this observation does not establish legitimacy.

options.text: The cache is definitely corrupt
options.explanation: One MAC can serve multiple IP addresses; the representation itself is valid.

options.text: ARP spoofing is possible, but the mapping alone is insufficient to establish it
options.explanation: Correct. A legitimate multi-address interface or proxy ARP can produce the same pattern. Compare trusted network configuration and packet evidence.

options.text: The manufacturer must have assigned duplicate MAC addresses
options.explanation: The cache does not prove that two physical interfaces exist or have identical factory addresses.

questions.workedExample: ARP records claimed IP-to-MAC mappings, not device identities or intent. Multiple addresses can belong to one interface, and a proxy can answer for other addresses. Forged ARP is another possibility. A diagnosis needs additional evidence. Properly authenticated encryption protects contents if interception occurs, while metadata and availability can remain exposed.

questions.prompt: You run a corporate LAN and want to protect users from ARP spoofing by another device on the same network. Which measures genuinely help? Select all that apply.

options.text: Correctly configured Dynamic ARP Inspection with trusted DHCP bindings or static ARP ACLs
options.explanation: Correct. Inspection rejects inconsistent ARP on protected untrusted ports. Coverage depends on trust boundaries, bindings and static-host configuration.

options.text: Using properly authenticated TLS, SSH or a VPN over the relevant traffic path
options.explanation: Correct. This protects application contents and integrity across that path; it does not stop ARP cache poisoning, traffic analysis or denial of service.

options.text: Increasing the ARP cache timeout so entries last longer
options.explanation: Spoofing works by *updating* existing entries with unsolicited replies, so a longer timeout doesn't help. It may even keep a poisoned entry around longer.

options.text: Splitting the network into smaller VLANs
options.explanation: Correct. ARP only works within a layer 2 domain, so smaller VLANs shrink the set of devices that can attack each other.

options.text: Changing the Wi-Fi password every month
options.explanation: The attacker in this scenario is already on the network, as a legitimate member. The password controls who joins, not what members can say in ARP.

questions.workedExample: DAI can reject forged ARP on protected ports. Authenticated encryption limits exposure of contents and undetected modification. Smaller VLANs reduce the set of reachable layer 2 peers. Extending a timeout does not authenticate updates, and password rotation alone does not constrain a member who remains authorised. None of these alone makes every interception consequence harmless.

lessons.title: Switch loops and root election
lessons.summary: Explain broadcast circulation and choose a spanning-tree root using the complete bridge ID.
lessons.body:
## The loop problem

Engineers like redundancy, so they connect switches in rings or meshes: if one link fails, another takes over. With plain switches this is a disaster.

Consider three switches in a triangle, and a host that sends one broadcast:

```
        S1
       /  \
     S2 -- S3
```

S1 floods it to S2 and S3. S2 floods its copy to S3; S3 floods its copy to S2. Each of those floods it back to S1, which floods again. Copies recirculate; branching topologies can also multiply them.

- Basic Ethernet frames have **no forwarding TTL**. A loop has no hop-count expiry, though congestion, faults or filtering can still discard frames.
- Repeated flooding can consume link capacity and cause a **broadcast storm**; the onset and severity depend on traffic and topology.
- MAC tables can **flap** as the same source arrives on different ports.
- Hosts may spend substantial resources processing unwanted broadcasts.

A single patch cable plugged into two wall ports on the same switch can take down an entire office this way.

## Spanning Tree Protocol

Classic **STP** (historically IEEE 802.1D) lets switches agree on a loop-free **tree** across the physical mesh, and block the remaining links. After a failure, the tree is recomputed; an eligible redundant port can become forwarding if a usable alternate path exists.

Switches exchange **BPDUs** (bridge protocol data units), using a default hello time of 2 seconds and the standard bridge-group multicast MAC `01:80:c2:00:00:00`. Each BPDU says, in effect, "I think the root is X, and my cost to reach it is C".

### Step 1: elect a root bridge

Every bridge has a **bridge ID**, combining a priority/system-ID field and a MAC address. The **lowest** ID wins. With equal priority/system-ID fields, the lowest MAC wins; this does not reliably indicate age or speed. Configure priorities to favour the intended root.

With the extended system ID, configurable priority occupies the upper four bits (steps of 4096, commonly default 32768); the lower 12 bits identify the relevant instance. In per-VLAN STP this is the VLAN ID, but it is not universally a VLAN number.

## Key takeaways
- Basic Ethernet has no forwarding hop count, so switching loops can cause storms.
- The lowest priority/system-ID and MAC combination becomes root.

questions.prompt: Someone plugs both ends of a patch cable into two ports on the same office switch, which isn't running spanning tree. Within seconds the whole office network is unusable. Why doesn't the looping traffic die out on its own?

options.text: Basic Ethernet has no forwarding TTL to expire a frame after a bounded number of hops
options.explanation: Correct. Copies can keep circulating until dropped or the loop is removed. Congestion or faults can discard frames, but there is no hop-count expiry.

options.text: The switch's MAC table is too small
options.explanation: The table does get confused (MAC table flapping), but even a huge table wouldn't stop broadcasts circulating. The root issue is that nothing limits a frame's lifetime.

options.text: The cable creates an electrical short that disables the switch
options.explanation: Plugging a cable into two ports is electrically fine. Each port sees a normal link. The problem is entirely logical: frames go round in a circle.

options.text: The frames' CRCs fail on every lap, causing retransmissions
options.explanation: The frames aren't corrupted; they are perfectly valid copies. Ethernet doesn't retransmit on CRC failure anyway.

questions.workedExample: A broadcast is flooded out eligible ports other than its ingress port. Copies returning through the cable can be flooded again. New traffic adds load, and source addresses can be learned on alternating ports. This can overwhelm the network, but severity is topology- and traffic-dependent. STP prevents forwarding loops; BPDU guard disables a guarded port when it receives a BPDU, not for every conceivable loop.

questions.prompt:
Four switches run STP. Which becomes the root bridge?

```
switch  priority  MAC
A       32768     00:00:0c:11:11:11
B       32768     00:00:0c:00:00:01
C       4096      f8:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff
D       32768     00:00:0c:00:00:00
```

Assume the same spanning-tree instance and equal extended system IDs.

options.text: A
options.explanation: A has default priority and neither the lowest priority nor the lowest MAC.

options.text: B
options.explanation: B's MAC is low, but D's is lower still, and in any case priority is compared before the MAC.

options.text: C
options.explanation: Correct. The bridge ID is priority first, then MAC. C's priority of 4096 beats 32768, so its high MAC doesn't matter.

options.text: D
options.explanation: D has the lowest MAC and would win if all priorities were equal. But the priority is the most significant part of the bridge ID, and C's is lower.

questions.workedExample:
Compare bridge IDs as (priority, MAC), lowest wins:

```
A (32768, 00:00:0c:11:11:11)
B (32768, 00:00:0c:00:00:01)
C ( 4096, f8:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff)  <- lowest
D (32768, 00:00:0c:00:00:00)
```

1. Lowest priority: C, with 4096.
2. The MAC only breaks ties between equal priorities.

This is why you set a low priority on the switch you *want* as root. Leave them all at default and D would win purely because it has the lowest MAC.

lessons.title: Spanning-tree ports and path cost
lessons.summary: Choose root and designated ports and trace the equal-cost triangle.
lessons.body:
### Step 2: each switch picks a root port

Every non-root switch chooses one **root port**: its port with the lowest total **path cost** to the root (the sum of the costs of every link on the way). Costs come from link speed; in the commonly used short path-cost table, 100 Mbit/s costs 19, 1 Gbit/s costs 4 and 10 Gbit/s costs 2. After equal root IDs and path costs, ties use the sender bridge ID, sender port ID, and finally local port ID. Costs may be configured; long path-cost values differ.

### Step 3: each link picks a designated port

On each segment, the port advertising the best root information becomes the **designated port**. With the same root ID, compare root path cost, then sender bridge ID and sender port ID. Root and designated ports forward data once the relevant state transitions have completed; a role alone does not imply immediate forwarding. In the simple point-to-point topology below, the root ends of inter-switch links are designated. Shared segments and multiple ports attached to one LAN segment need the full port-role rules.

In this stable classic-STP example, an enabled redundant port that is neither root nor designated is **blocked**: it still listens to BPDUs but forwards no data. During convergence, even a root or designated port can temporarily be listening or learning.

### The triangle, worked

All three links are 1 Gbit/s (cost 4), all priority/system-ID fields are equal, and the MAC ordering is S1 < S2 < S3.

| Switch | Cost to root | Root port |
|---|---|---|
| S1 | 0 (root) | none |
| S2 | 4 | to S1 |
| S3 | 4 | to S1 |

The S2–S3 link: both ends have cost 4, so the tie goes to the lower bridge ID, S2. S2's end is designated; S3's end is neither root nor designated, so it **blocks**.

```
        S1 (root)
       /  \
      R    R
     S2 -D-X- S3
 R: root port   D: designated
 X: blocked
```

If the S1–S3 link fails, S3 stops receiving BPDUs from S1, its blocked port becomes its new root port, and traffic flows via S2.

## Key takeaways
- Non-root switches choose a root port using full path cost and tie-breakers.
- A designated port forwards for each segment; blocking a redundant endpoint removes the loop.

questions.prompt:
Three switches run STP. S1 is root. Link costs:

```
S1 -- S2 : 100 Mbit/s, cost 19
S1 -- S3 : 1 Gbit/s,   cost 4
S2 -- S3 : 1 Gbit/s,   cost 4
```

Which port ends up blocked? Assume three point-to-point links, one spanning-tree instance and a stable topology.

options.text: S3's port on the S2–S3 link
options.explanation: S3 reaches the root at cost 4, better than S2's best of 8, so S3's end of the S2–S3 link is designated and forwards.

options.text: S2's port on the S1–S2 link
options.explanation: Correct. S2's best path is via S3 (4 + 4 = 8 < 19), so its root port faces S3. On the S1–S2 link, S1 is designated (it is root), and S2's end is neither root nor designated: blocked.

options.text: S1's port on the S1–S2 link
options.explanation: On this triangle's point-to-point links, S1's ends are designated. S2 blocks its direct root link because its path through S3 costs less.

options.text: None: there is no loop because the links have different speeds
options.explanation: Speed doesn't affect whether there's a loop: three switches in a triangle always form one. Costs only decide *which* link gets blocked.

questions.workedExample: Compare S2's paths, using the supplied costs: the direct slow link costs 19, while the route through S3 costs 8. S2 therefore chooses its port toward S3 as root port. S3 chooses its direct port toward S1. S1's ends are designated on these point-to-point links. On the S1–S2 link, S2's end is neither its root port nor designated, so it blocks in the stable topology. The tree selects the cheaper route, even though it passes through another switch.

lessons.title: STP recovery, guards and alternatives
lessons.summary: Understand default STP timers, qualified RSTP recovery and safer redundant designs.
lessons.body:
### STP convergence: the slow part

Classic STP is cautious. A port moving towards forwarding passes through **listening** (15 s) and **learning** (15 s) states, the "forward delay", so the whole network can settle before any data flows. If a failure is detected only by BPDUs stopping, the switch first waits up to the 20-second **max age**. With these default timers, a transition can therefore take **30 to 50 seconds**; actual recovery depends on the failure and topology.

**RSTP** (originally 802.1w, incorporated into 802.1D-2004 and subsequently the combined 802.1Q bridging standard) enables faster transitions. Neighbours negotiate directly with a proposal and agreement handshake, alternate ports are pre-computed as backups, and suitable point-to-point transitions can complete in under a second. Failure detection and legacy neighbours can still introduce delays. **MSTP** (802.1s) runs separate trees for groups of VLANs, so different VLANs can use different links.

### Edge ports and guards

- An **edge port** (Cisco: PortFast) connects to a host, not a switch, so it skips the forward delay. With classic default timers, forwarding can otherwise wait 30 seconds after link-up; DHCP behaviour depends on client retries.
- **BPDU guard** shuts down an edge port that receives a BPDU, protecting the host-port assumption when BPDUs arrive. It is not a detector for every possible loop or silent device.
- **Root guard** stops a port from accepting a better root, so a misconfigured or malicious switch with priority 0 can't hijack the root and drag traffic through itself.

> [!tip] Diagnose before changing topology
> Inspect root IDs, port roles, link status and counters. A unidirectional link can require loop guard or an appropriate link-detection mechanism; the applicable feature depends on the failure and equipment.

## Beyond spanning tree

A spanning tree leaves some redundant paths unavailable for data within that instance; the unused fraction depends on topology. Alternatives can make more paths available:

- **Link aggregation** (LACP, 802.1AX) bundles parallel links into one logical link that STP sees as a single port, so eligible members can share flows. Hashing and the workload determine utilisation; one flow normally stays on one member.
- **MLAG** coordinates a link aggregation across two switches; details and failure behaviour are implementation-dependent.
- **Routed leaf-spine designs** can use ECMP across multiple equal-cost paths. IP TTL bounds a packet's lifetime in a forwarding loop; ECMP does not guarantee equal utilisation or that every link is busy. Layer 2 services may be extended over VXLAN.

## Key takeaways
- Classic default timers can introduce 30–50-second transitions.
- RSTP, edge-port guards, aggregation and routed multipath need their own failure and configuration assumptions.

What's the cause and fix? Assume the default 15-second forward delay and an ordinary host-facing port.

options.text: The port is passing through STP's listening and learning states; configure desk ports as edge ports (PortFast)
options.explanation: Correct. With these defaults, listening and learning each last 15 seconds. An appropriately configured host edge port can forward immediately.

options.text: The DHCP server is overloaded; add a second one
options.explanation: The stated STP defaults can withhold forwarding for 30 seconds. Check port states to confirm that explanation; timing alone does not exclude other faults.

options.text: Auto-negotiation is slow; hard-code the speed and duplex
options.explanation: A link light alone does not diagnose negotiation details, but the specified classic STP timing explains this delay. Forcing one side can create a duplex mismatch.

options.text: The laptop's ARP cache is stale; it must time out first
options.explanation: A stale next-hop mapping can affect many destinations, particularly through a gateway. It does not itself explain the specified STP listening/learning delay; confirm port states and neighbour information.

Configure genuine host ports as edge/PortFast ports. BPDU guard disables a guarded port when a BPDU arrives, helping enforce the host-only assumption. It does not detect every silent switch or loop.

questions.prompt: Which statements comparing classic STP (802.1D-1998) with RSTP (802.1w) are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: Classic STP can take 30–50 seconds to restore connectivity after a failure
options.explanation: Correct. Up to 20 s of max age before noticing an indirect failure, then 15 s listening and 15 s learning.

options.text: RSTP can use proposal/agreement on suitable point-to-point links to avoid classic forward-delay waits
options.explanation: Correct. Rapid transitions depend on port roles and synchronisation. Failure detection, shared media and legacy neighbours can still require timers.

options.text: RSTP lets all redundant links carry traffic at the same time
options.explanation: RSTP still selects a tree per instance. Link aggregation, multiple instances or routed ECMP can provide more usable paths, but do not guarantee every physical link carries data.

options.text: Both elect a root bridge using the lowest bridge ID
options.explanation: Correct. RSTP keeps the same root election and cost model; what changed is how quickly ports transition.

questions.workedExample: With classic default timers, a transition can require two 15-second forward delays, with up to 20 seconds of ageing in relevant failure cases. RSTP retains bridge-ID election but adds roles and handshakes for faster transitions. Sub-second recovery is possible, not universal. Redundant non-forwarding ports still exist within an instance.

questions.prompt: All switches have equal STP priority/system-ID fields. A newly connected switch advertises a lower bridge ID, and status commands confirm that it became root. Which configuration would prevent that port from accepting an unexpected superior root?

options.text: Increase the MAC table size
options.explanation: The forwarding table size does not control root election.

options.text: Configure intended root priorities and enable root guard on that boundary port
options.explanation: Correct. Priorities make the intended election explicit; root guard blocks a boundary port from accepting a superior root.

options.text: Lower the new switch's numeric priority
options.explanation: That makes its bridge ID more favourable, increasing its chance of becoming root.

options.text: Enable all redundant ports for forwarding without STP
options.explanation: That can introduce forwarding loops and does not enforce the intended root.

Set lower numeric priorities on intended root and backup bridges and use root guard where a superior root must not appear. Becoming root does not imply all data traverses that switch: forwarding follows the resulting tree, and a singly connected root cannot be an intermediate path between other switches.

lessons.title: Hamming distance and parity
lessons.summary: Separate detection and correction guarantees and test parity’s blind spots.
lessons.body:
Physical links can introduce errors through noise, interference or equipment faults. Error rates depend on the link, operating conditions and coding; there is no single Ethernet or wireless rate. A reliability design must consider two distinct functions:
1. **Detect** that a frame was damaged, so it isn't delivered as if it were good.
2. **Recover**, either by fixing the error in place (forward error correction) or by sending the data again (**ARQ**, automatic repeat request).

This unit starts with the distance between valid codewords and the simplest detection code, parity. Later units examine stronger checks and retransmission strategies.

## The idea behind every check

The sender computes a few redundant bits from the data and sends them along. The receiver recomputes them from what arrived. A mismatch means something changed.

How good a code is depends on its **Hamming distance**: the minimum number of bit flips needed to turn one valid codeword (a bit pattern the code allows) into another. From the distance you can read off how many flipped bits the code is guaranteed to catch or repair:

```formula reference
t_detect = d − 1
t_correct = ⌊(d − 1) / 2⌋
where
d: the code's minimum Hamming distance, a whole number of bits
t_detect: the largest number of flipped bits that is always detected
t_correct: the largest number of flipped bits that can always be corrected
⌊ ⌋: the floor function: round down to the nearest whole number (⌊1.5⌋ = 1)
In words: detection works while damage cannot turn one valid codeword into another; guaranteed correction requires the damaged word to remain closer to its original than to every alternative.
```

For example, a code with distance 3 detects up to 2 flipped bits, or corrects 1, because one flipped bit still leaves it closer to its original than to any other valid codeword.

For a given worst-case number of bit errors, correction requires a larger minimum distance than detection. These are alternative decoding guarantees; a distance-3 correcting decoder cannot also promise to identify every two-bit error as uncorrectable.

## Parity

One **parity bit** makes the number of 1s even (even parity). Distance is 2, so it catches any single-bit error, and any odd number of flips, but misses every even number. Two flips in a byte cancel out.

A **burst error** spans from the first changed bit to the last; intermediate bits need not all change. Parity misses bursts containing an even number of flips, so it cannot guarantee detection of even a two-bit burst.

## Key takeaways
- Minimum distance bounds alternative detection and correction guarantees.
- Even parity catches odd numbers of flipped bits but misses even numbers.
